attempts.answer:
Summary
Traditional broadcasters have avoided fully replicating several SVOD production and distribution strategies—most notably large-scale algorithmic personalization as a loyalty engine, platform-led vertical integration and micro-operations without commercial breaks, and data-driven, attention-weighted development loops centered on originals and independent producers—because linear scheduling, advertiser dependence, legacy rights and organizational structures, and regulatory/industry norms create significant frictions and risks. Where broadcasters have moved, it has often been to hybrid or BVOD strategies that mirror linear programs rather than SVOD’s library-first, recommendation-driven model. <cite id="8f92a024-2">In SVOD, planned linear flow is replaced by big-data and personalization algorithms to build loyalty and recommend content</cite> <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVODs treat originals as brand-building, bespoke content to cultivate niche audiences via personalized discoverability</cite> <cite id="8ce6bd84-0">Broadcasters complement linear offerings with content libraries and originals, but outcomes depend on content/system quality</cite> <cite id="ee7dd900-0">User studies repeatedly tie Netflix’s personalization and recommendation UX to continuance intentions and satisfaction</cite> <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix’s recommendation systems evolved via a million-dollar competition and extensive data-driven engineering to maintain engagement</cite> <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">Parrot Analytics-style attention metrics (engagement, repeat viewing, social/Google activity) redefine SVOD audience value beyond TAMs</cite> <cite id="8f92a024-3">Some broadcasters repurpose on-air content to podcasts but retain integrated, archival models rather than standalone, algorithmically curated originals</cite>.

Production strategies SVOD adopted that broadcasters have not fully embraced
- Algorithmic personalization and recommendation systems as central to development and retention:
  <cite id="ee7dd900-0">Netflix users repeatedly identify “good recommendations” and UI/UX personalization as core reasons for reuse; personalization indirectly drives continuance via habit, and high usage (>3x/week) is reported among respondents</cite>. 
  <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix’s recommendation system became a data-driven R&D focal point (the Netflix Prize), iteratively improving prediction and engagement after users typically viewed only 10–20 titles in 60–90 seconds of searching</cite>. 
  <cite id="ee7dd900-1">SVOD platforms act as gatekeepers that tailor home pages to users’ algorithmic profiles, with “infinite” catalogs that still deliver ‘more of the same’ via effective personalization software</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-2">Linear TV’s “flow TV” scheduling built loyalty, while SVOD replaces planned blocks with algorithmic personalization and big-data-driven curation</cite> <cite id="ee7dd900-2">SVOD interfaces must mitigate choice overload, emphasizing familiarity to reduce anxiety and improve perceived usefulness and satisfaction</cite>. Organizational path dependence in linear production and advertising-supported scheduling makes algorithmic personalization less central than ad-insertion and promo-driven discovery.

- Originals-led brand building with independent producers and platformized workflows:
  <cite id="8f92a024-0">Spanish SVOD originals reveal a shift toward cooperation between independent production companies and platforms, with no in-house production by platforms and atomized production roles</cite>. 
  <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVODs prioritize original content to signal curatorial ethos and brand identity; originals span developed, acquired, co-produced, and licensed categories to build a distinctive library</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-0">European broadcasters complement catch-up libraries with originals, creating a streaming consumption mix with substantial usage</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-4">SVODs’ serialised fiction became decisive in on-demand consumption, while conventional TV retained reality formats</cite> <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD’s planned-flow replacement and atomization of production roles reposition producers, platforms, and consumers relative to traditional TV</cite>. Many broadcasters still rely on legacy in-house studios and advertiser-aligned schedules; shifting to independent-producer partnerships for originals carries brand dilution and distribution risk that conflicts with linear identity.

- Data-to-decision loops: attention-weighted metrics and social amplification:
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD audience value is fragmented, weighted, volatile, and adhered; Parrot Analytics’ approach weights attention by internal (frequency, intensity, repeat viewing) and external signals (social posts, Google searches, downloads) to assign value beyond TAM reach</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-2">Broadcasters increasingly look to YouTube, TikTok, and OTT platforms for mobile, on-demand content and algorithmic targeting, but must reinvent content strategies and overcome systemic barriers</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8ce6bd84-3">AI and data-driven automation are present but evolving in radio/broadcasts, hindered by infrastructure, capacity, and policy gaps that slow full integration into core workflows</cite>. Legacy measurement (TAMs) and advertiser tolerance for broad demos slow adoption of granular, engagement-centric metrics tied to platform-side A/B testing and slate optimization.

- Micro-operations and platform-controlled delivery:
  <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD replaces traditional flow with on-demand content and personalization algorithms to recommend and make content visible, shifting strategic positioning of producers and distributors</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-0">Content library UX and quality drive usage and word-of-mouth; platform-controlled libraries can be advertising-financed or subscription-based, and their design matters for outcomes</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-3">When extending content digitally, some broadcasters repurpose existing programs and retain integrated production models, positioning podcasts as archival extensions rather than standalone SVOD originals with algorithmic discoverability</cite>. Linear schedule economics and live-event carriage commitments make micro-ops and commercial-break–free micro-episodes less central than time-shifting linear blocks and ad-supported VOD tie-ins.

Distribution strategies SVOD adopted that broadcasters have not fully embraced
- First-party OTT app control and direct-to-consumer branding:
  <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVODs deploy explicit content strategies through originals to forge brand identity and curate narrative trends, reflecting platform control over interface and curation</cite>. 
  <cite id="ee7dd900-1">SVOD “invisibility” elements (algorithms, software) are crucial to ensure personalization effectiveness, embedding the brand as gatekeeper and curator</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-4">European broadcasters’ SVOD hybrids remain library-plus-originals overlays rather than replacing linear identity, and outcomes hinge on brand perception and system quality</cite>. Advertiser-driven identities and multiplatform obligations make radical app-first branding more risky than incremental overlays.

- Recommendation-driven libraries vs. BVOD mirroring of linear schedules:
  <cite id="8f92a024-4">BVOD services generally highlight linear programming and use discoverability strategies aligned with maximizing linear audience, whereas SVODs personalize and curate libraries to cultivate niche audiences and retain subscribers</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-0">Hulu’s shift from curating catch-up to a popular SVOD provider exemplifies platform strategies that mix library curation with originals and advertising/subscription hybrids</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD relies on big data and personalization to build loyalty, while conventional TV retains planned-flow strategies and reality formats to retain mass audiences</cite>. Linear scheduling and advertiser-supported models incentivize program blocks and promo-driven discovery rather than algorithmic personalization as a primary retention lever.

- No-commercial-break micro-operations and binge pacing:
  <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD enables planned-flow obsolescence and replaces it with on-demand, algorithmically guided visibility that supports micro-ops and binge-friendly serialization</cite>. 
  <cite id="8f92a024-4">Serialised fiction became decisive for SVOD, while conventional TV emphasizes reality formats</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVOD’s originals are deployed to signal curatorial ethos and brand identity, which conflicts with advertiser- and break-tolerant brand-building norms</cite>. Advertiser protection of commercial breaks and live-event carriage create structural resistance to ad-free micro-ops and to pacing that maximizes session friction for retention.

- Data-driven slate optimization and experimentation at internet scale:
  <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix’s competition-driven refinement of recommendation systems addresses engagement decay quickly (users searched ~60–90 seconds, viewed ~10–20 titles), pushing continuous algorithmic experimentation</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD audience value is measured by engagement and density (e.g., Netflix’s metrics) and Parrot-like weighting by attention signals beyond TAMs</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8ce6bd84-3">AI adoption in broadcast is constrained by infrastructure, capacity building, and policy support, which slows integration into core scheduling and development</cite>. Legacy rights, residuals, and union constraints also complicate rapid A/B testing and slate optimization that would require new rights pools and workflow governance.

What explains these strategic omissions: constraints and organizational factors
- Linear scheduling norms and advertiser dependence:
  <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD replaces planned-flow blocks with algorithmic personalization and big-data-driven recommendation to build loyalty; conventional TV clings to flow strategies and reality formats</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-4">The shift to SVOD made serialised fiction central, while conventional TV retained reality’s dominance</cite>. Linear advertisers and networks rely on live and scheduled promos and commercial breaks; replacing them with ad-free micro-ops and algorithmic personalization undermines advertiser business models and brand identity.

- Regulatory and industry infrastructure:
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-2">Traditional TV must digitize infrastructure and reinvent content strategies to remain resonant, leveraging YouTube/TikTok/OTT for mobile-friendly content and algorithmic targeting</cite>. <cite id="8ce6bd84-3">AI and automation are present but evolving, hindered by infrastructure, capacity, and policy gaps that slow full integration into core broadcasting functions</cite>. Broadcasters face fragmented rights, carriage, and indecency regimes plus live-event protections that complicate global SVOD rollout and ad-supported experimentation.

- Brand and commercial risk:
  <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVODs deploy originals to craft brand identity and curate narratives; originals are a marketing construct with platform-specific definitions</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-0">SVOD originals rely on independent production partnerships, signaling a departure from in-house production</cite>. For legacy broadcasters, original-led data-to-decision loops risk alienating advertiser or studio partners and diluting brand identity; incremental BVOD overlays reduce risk while preserving linear scale.

- Scale, cost, and measurement:
  <cite id="ee7dd900-0">Personalization significantly impacts satisfaction and continuance; Netflix users explicitly cite recommendations and UI/UX as key drivers</cite>. <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix invested heavily in recommendation engineering (e.g., the Netflix Prize) to overcome engagement decay within seconds of browsing</cite>. <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD value depends on weighted, volatile, adhered audiences measured by engagement and attention beyond TAMs</cite>. Broadcasters face higher marginal costs for originals and data infrastructure, plus advertiser reliance on coarse TAMs that disincentivize granular engagement measurement and rapid iteration.

Title: The production of Spanish fiction series for SVOD: evolution, trends and strategies
Snippet: The consolidation of digital television via subscription video on demand (SVOD) services has created an unprecedented increase in the consumption of serialised TV shows, which has had direct consequences on the content production sector. Faced with an increasingly demanding, hyperconnected and discerning audience and a supply of content never previously seen, television production and distribution strategies are involved in a process of change and adaptation. This paper seeks to analyse the production of Spanish television series created to be distributed on SVOD platforms. The aim is to know the role that production companies play in the creation of television series for SVOD so as to identify strategies and cooperative alliances between production companies and platforms and to detect possible patterns and trends in the operations of the audiovisual market. Using a mixed methodology that combines quantitative study with qualitative data analysis, the 88 Spanish TV series and miniseries that premiered on SVOD platforms from 2016 to 2021 are analysed, taking as a starting point the year in which these platforms began operating in Spain. The results confirm a trend towards cooperation between independent production companies and the platforms themselves, while no presence of in-house production is observed. Likewise, the atomisation of the role of production companies in the context of SVOD is shown, a phenomenon that already existed in generalist television production.

Snippet: In the era of SVOD services, original content is key. Historically, streaming services' catalogs were predominantly comprised of licensed programs. Focusing on 'original content' is especially instructive as it sheds light on a streaming service's curatorial and programming strategies. It offers insights into a platform's content development ethosessentially, the brand identity it endeavors to forge and the narrative trends it deems most compelling. As Lotz argues: 'Distinguishing bespoke content developed specifically for the SVOD is important because services are able to deploy explicit content strategies through these titles'. Yet, the concept of 'original content', often ubiquitously deployed within the media industry, eludes a simplistic definition and warrants further elucidation. As Matthew Ball (2018) contends: '"Original" isn't a technical definition but a marketing one. And thus not only is the definition of "Original" vague, it also differs from network to network'. In academic circles, 'original content' is broadly classified into four distinct categories (Afilipoaie et al., 2021;Ball 2018) : (1) developed originals, that is, bespoke content that is commissioned and produced directly for a streaming service; (2) acquired originals, i.e., content that is purchased after production or to resume production; (3) co-productions between a streaming service and a national broadcaster; and (4) licensed originals, which refer to works not initially made for a streaming service but that have been granted exclusive online distribution rights.

Snippet: The arrival of Netflix in 2015, together with the first á la carte actions of Movistar+, marked the beginning of a new television era in Spain orientated towards on-demand consumption. A year later, HBO and Amazon Prime Video, as well as the rest of the platforms that have successively joined the on-demand service, ended up altering both the way of consuming television and the usual programming process and, by extension, the production of television content. The flow TV, or planned flow, which Raymond Williams (1974) defined as the strategy based on the programming blocks of television channels whose intention was to retain and build audience loyalty, loses its meaning in the context of on-demand television, in which big data and personalisation algorithms are the only valid flows for building loyalty, recommending or making attractive content visible to digital audiences (Heredia-Ruiz, Quirós-Ramírez & Quiceno-Castañeda, 2021). Accordingly, in recent years the planned flow that had characterised television strategy almost from its origins has been replaced by the offer of on-demand content, modifying the strategic positioning of the different multimedia groups, television channels, production companies and, of course, consumers themselves. 

In a changing television scenario, in which video on demand appears to lead the race for content, new interests, formulas and strategies are emerging that condition the way in which content is created, produced and distributed (Telkmann, 2021;Doyle, 2016;Smith & Hendricks, 2010). Television series, in particular, are presented as the central element in the offer of SVOD platforms, so it could be said that the rise of the serialised fiction format has been decisive in the transition towards on-demand consumption, while other formats such as reality shows have gained great weight in conventional television (Villegas, 2018;Hidalgo-Marí et al., 2021). 

This paper includes research carried out from the perspective of content production that provides data on production companies, platforms and production strategies detected in the recent scenario of Spanish serialised fiction created specifically for SVOD. The study aims to establish a state of the art that goes a step further into the study of production and its different formulations as a determining element of the general offer of series on SVOD platforms.
</snippet>

Title: Radio’s Role in Digital Information Dissemination
Snippet: The findings reveal that Motion Radio adopts a selective content curation strategy, prioritizing informative, educational, and socially relevant programs over purely entertainment-oriented broadcasts. Podcast content is primarily derived from recorded on-air programs and repackaged for digital distribution, demonstrating an integrated production model in which existing broadcast workflows are optimized to serve dual platforms. This approach reflects organizational efficiency in the absence of a dedicated podcast team, while simultaneously presenting managerial challenges related to limited human resources and time constraints. 

Furthermore, podcasts are positioned as an extension of Motion Radio's institutional identity as an information-oriented broadcaster. Rather than functioning solely as archival storage, podcasts are strategically utilized to reach digitally oriented audience segments who may not regularly engage with traditional radio. Overall, the table highlights how podcasting operates as both a technological adaptation and a strategic communication response within Motion Radio's media convergence framework. The first finding indicates that the development of podcasts by Motion Radio is driven by the need to overcome the limitations of radio broadcasts, which are ephemeral and cannot be replayed. Informants emphasized that much informative content considered valuable for listeners may be missed if it is only broadcast live. Therefore, podcasts are utilized as a means to extend content accessibility, allowing audiences to listen to the content again at different times. 

The second finding relates to the podcast content curation strategy. Motion Radio does not upload all radio broadcast materials into podcast format; instead, it selectively curates specific content. Priority is given to informative, educational, and listener-relevant materials, such as topics on health, careers, public policy, and social issues. In contrast, light entertainment-oriented content tends not to be converted into podcasts, as it is considered to have limited long-term utility. 

The third finding shows that the primary source of Motion Radio's podcast content comes from live (on-air) broadcasts. Podcasts are not produced as entirely separate content, but rather as recordings and repackaged versions of talk shows or dialogues that have already been aired. This practice indicates that podcasts are positioned as an extension of radio broadcasts rather than as standalone media products. 

The fourth finding concerns the podcast production model implemented by Motion Radio. Podcast production is carried out in an integrated manner with radio broadcast production, without a dedicated podcast team.

Title: Datacasting: TikTok’s Algorithmic Flow as Televisual Experience
Snippet: By simplifying the recommendation process by implementing automated algorithmic feeds, social media platforms such as the aforementioned have managed to attract more and more viewers throughout the years, with a study conducted by Deloitte in 2023 confirming that people belonging to Generation Z (1997)(1998)(1999)(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009) have started preferring video content available on social media to traditional television (Westcott  et al., 2023). Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, 2015, p. 2) faced by users on traditional subscription video on demand (SVOD) services. 

As we have seen, personalisation is at the centre of contemporary flow experiences, in that most platforms and services that currently offer audiovisual content are algorithm-based. What this entails is that home pages within streaming services are built according to users' algorithmic identities (Cheney-Lippold, 2011), and that these services act as gatekeepers, only showing subscribers the content they deem appropriate (Van Esler, 2021). In analysing SVOD platforms, Cox highlighted the importance of focusing on two distinct aspects of the services: televisible elements, which refer to visual elements within the interface, and invisual elements, algorithms, and softwares that influence the way in which users interact with the service (2018). The former become fundamental in shaping user experience on the platform: As highlighted by Johnson (2019), SVOD services provide users with (seemingly) infinite rows of content, which provide the feeling of choosing from an ample catalogue, although the platform algorithms are merely offering "more of the same" (Lüders & Shanke Sundet, 2022). The latter, on the other hand, are one of the key components of datacasting experiences, in that they are crucial in ensuring that the personalisation that services enact is effective.

Title: When the Known Well May Sell
Snippet: While Streaming Video on Demand (SVOD) consumers may express a desire for unlimited new and novel choices, excess choice can cause anxiety and choice overload. Familiarity tends to override potential choice overload effects and non-familiarity tends to exacerbate negative effects associated with too much choice, which has implications for purveyors of not only SVOD systems but other digital applications with similar recommendation systems, such as music streaming and podcasts, to emphasise choices that are likely to have familiarity to consumers, especially when interfaces themselves may be unfamiliar.

Title: The show must go on(line): the impact of content and system quality on the usage of television streaming content libraries
Snippet: The main aim of this paper is to analyze the influencing factors of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes of content library usage.Content libraries (sometimes also called media libraries, Gutzeit et al., 2021) can be defined as closed television station portals structured like libraries with professionally produced (long-format) content; the majority of content is repurposed from the linear television programming schedule (Lobato, 2019;Lotz, 2017).Such content libraries have become a global phenomenon.In countries such as the UK, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Argentina, or Japan, television broadcasters complement their linear offerings via Internet Protocol-distributed, advertising-financed and/or subscription-based content libraries (see examples in Table A1 in the Appendix).These offerings have become a relevant part of the streaming video competition landscape.Hulu, which started by curating the catch-up offerings of U.S. television channels, counts among the most popular SVoD providers, with 28% of U.S. adults tuning in at least every week (Morning Consult, 2022).

In the European context, several television groups have complemented their catch-up content libraries with original content, establishing those offers as part of the streaming consumption mix.Our research focuses on the German media market, one of the largest markets for SVoD in the world (Rahe et al., 2021).The German media system is characterized by strong competition between private and public service broadcasters, which extends to the SVoD market, with both groups attracting substantial usage of their content library offerings (ARD/ZDF Forschungskommission, 2023).Also, private and public groups both invest substantial sums in content production and content libraries (ARD, 2023;Meier, 2023), making these well-developed offerings a suitable object of investigation.As a result, content library usage is well established: 39% of Germans use content libraries on a daily or weekly basis (ARD/ZDF Forschungskommission, 2023; Schauerte et al., 2021).

Because our aim is to analyze attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, actual usage and word of mouth recommendation (behavioral outcomes) as well as brand perception (attitudinal outcome) serve as our dependent variables.

Snippet: Based on the analysis, we conclude that a revised concept of audience in the context of SVOD should consider a number of aspects: -It is constructed from an enormous volume of data whose main characteristic is its fragmentation (fragmented audience). -Audience research in this context involves interpreting and assigning a value to each new audience dimension arising from online consumption (weighted audience) and not just accumulating data. -The volatility inherent in these platform audiences, jumping easily between content and services -a volatile or 'gaseous' audience, using the term in Callejo-Gallego (2019)-, suggests that weight should be given to what is chosen and the quality of such choices, thereby producing new audience dimensions based on the connection established with content (adhered audience).

Given this revised concept of SVOD audience (fragmented, weighted, volatile and adhered), this study concludes that new dimensions above and beyond data provided by TAMs should be included. Such new dimensions are based on the premise that the value of the audience is not just its size, but also its engagement (users' involvement with content) and its depth of attention (audience density, to use Netflix's term). In assigning value to audience attention, the methodology used by Parrot Analytics, which takes us into the field of big data, opens up an interesting line of research: varying the weighting based on users' level of effort, both internally (frequency, intensity and repeat viewing) and externally (posts on social media, information searches in Google, illegal downloads).

  <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD audience value is fragmented, weighted, volatile, and adhered; Parrot Analytics’ approach weights attention by internal (frequency, intensity, repeat viewing) and external signals (social posts, Google searches, downloads) to assign value beyond TAM reach</cite>.

  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVOD’s originals are deployed to signal curatorial ethos and brand identity, which conflicts with advertiser- and break-tolerant brand-building norms</cite>. - Data-driven slate optimization and experimentation at internet scale:
  <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix’s competition-driven refinement of recommendation systems addresses engagement decay quickly (users searched ~60–90 seconds, viewed ~10–20 titles), pushing continuous algorithmic experimentation</cite>. 
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD audience value is measured by engagement and density (e.g., Netflix’s metrics) and Parrot-like weighting by attention signals beyond TAMs</cite>. 
  Why broadcasters did not fully adopt: <cite id="8ce6bd84-3">AI adoption in broadcast is constrained by infrastructure, capacity building, and policy support, which slows integration into core scheduling and development</cite>. What explains these strategic omissions: constraints and organizational factors
- Linear scheduling norms and advertiser dependence:
  <cite id="8f92a024-2">SVOD replaces planned-flow blocks with algorithmic personalization and big-data-driven recommendation to build loyalty; conventional TV clings to flow strategies and reality formats</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-4">The shift to SVOD made serialised fiction central, while conventional TV retained reality’s dominance</cite>.   <cite id="8ce6bd84-2">Traditional TV must digitize infrastructure and reinvent content strategies to remain resonant, leveraging YouTube/TikTok/OTT for mobile-friendly content and algorithmic targeting</cite>. <cite id="8ce6bd84-3">AI and automation are present but evolving, hindered by infrastructure, capacity, and policy gaps that slow full integration into core broadcasting functions</cite>. Broadcasters face fragmented rights, carriage, and indecency regimes plus live-event protections that complicate global SVOD rollout and ad-supported experimentation.

- Brand and commercial risk:
  <cite id="8f92a024-1">SVODs deploy originals to craft brand identity and curate narratives; originals are a marketing construct with platform-specific definitions</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-0">SVOD originals rely on independent production partnerships, signaling a departure from in-house production</cite>. For legacy broadcasters, original-led data-to-decision loops risk alienating advertiser or studio partners and diluting brand identity; incremental BVOD overlays reduce risk while preserving linear scale.

- Scale, cost, and measurement:
  <cite id="ee7dd900-0">Personalization significantly impacts satisfaction and continuance; Netflix users explicitly cite recommendations and UI/UX as key drivers</cite>. <cite id="ee7dd900-4">Netflix invested heavily in recommendation engineering (e.g., the Netflix Prize) to overcome engagement decay within seconds of browsing</cite>. <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">SVOD value depends on weighted, volatile, adhered audiences measured by engagement and attention beyond TAMs</cite>. - Partial adaptations and limits:
  <cite id="8ce6bd84-2">Some broadcasters (e.g., tvOne) have converged by leveraging YouTube as a secondary channel to bypass coverage limits, diversify revenue, and use algorithmic targeting, integrating transmedia storytelling and digital metrics</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-3">Others repurpose on-air content into podcast formats as an integrated extension of broadcast rather than standalone SVOD originals, reflecting limited human resources and time constraints</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-0">In Spain, SVODs drive independent-producer collaborations with no in-house production, a model many broadcasters have not fully replicated</cite>. <cite id="8f92a024-4">Across Europe, public and private broadcasters invest in content libraries and originals, but outcomes depend on brand perception and system quality, underscoring partial adoption rather than wholesale SVOD replication</cite>.

SVOD’s competitive advantages—algorithmic personalization, originals-led brand building with independent producers, engagement-weighted data loops, and platform-controlled micro-ops—are not fully replicated by broadcasters due to structural and strategic frictions. <cite id="8f92a024-2">Where broadcasters adopt SVOD-like tactics, they often blend library curation with originals while retaining linear scheduling and brand commitments</cite> <cite id="ee7dd900-0">and personalization remains a key driver of continuance in subscription services</cite>. <cite id="8ce6bd84-1">Only those willing to integrate attention-centric metrics and transmedia distribution at platform scale are beginning to narrow the gap</cite>. Title: Streaming Diversité: Exploring representations within French-language scripted series on Canadian SVOD services
Snippet: In the era of SVOD services, original content is key. Historically, streaming services' catalogs were predominantly comprised of licensed programs. However, with the proliferation of platforms, SVOD services started prioritizing original content (Lotz, 2022;Lotz and Lobato, 2023). Focusing on 'original content' is especially instructive as it sheds light on a streaming service's curatorial and programming strategies. It offers insights into a platform's content development ethosessentially, the brand identity it endeavors to forge and the narrative trends it deems most compelling. As Lotz argues: 'Distinguishing bespoke content developed specifically for the SVOD is important because services are able to deploy explicit content strategies through these titles'. (2022: 9) Furthermore, because of the specific affordances of internet distribution (Lotz, 2017;Lotz and Lobato, 2023), studying original productions is particularly instrumental in understanding the 'new kinds of creative possibilities for creators […], [and] modes of storytelling the affordances of SVOD allow' (Lotz and Lobato, 2023: 4). 

Yet, the concept of 'original content', often ubiquitously deployed within the media industry, eludes a simplistic definition and warrants further elucidation. As Matthew Ball (2018) contends: '"Original" isn't a technical definition but a marketing one. And thus not only is the definition of "Original" vague, it also differs from network to network'. In academic circles, 'original content' is broadly classified into four distinct categories (Afilipoaie et al., 2021;Ball 2018) : (1) developed originals, that is, bespoke content that is commissioned and produced directly for a streaming service; (2) acquired originals, i.e., content that is purchased after production or to resume production; (3) co-productions between a streaming service and a national broadcaster; and (4) licensed originals, which refer to works not initially made for a streaming service but that have been granted exclusive online distribution rights.

Title: The production of Spanish fiction series for SVOD: evolution, trends and strategies
Snippet: The arrival of Netflix in 2015, together with the first á la carte actions of Movistar+, marked the beginning of a new television era in Spain orientated towards on-demand consumption. A year later, HBO and Amazon Prime Video, as well as the rest of the platforms that have successively joined the on-demand service, ended up altering both the way of consuming television and the usual programming process and, by extension, the production of television content. The flow TV, or planned flow, which Raymond Williams (1974) defined as the strategy based on the programming blocks of television channels whose intention was to retain and build audience loyalty, loses its meaning in the context of on-demand television, in which big data and personalisation algorithms are the only valid flows for building loyalty, recommending or making attractive content visible to digital audiences (Heredia-Ruiz, Quirós-Ramírez & Quiceno-Castañeda, 2021). Accordingly, in recent years the planned flow that had characterised television strategy almost from its origins has been replaced by the offer of on-demand content, modifying the strategic positioning of the different multimedia groups, television channels, production companies and, of course, consumers themselves. 

In a changing television scenario, in which video on demand appears to lead the race for content, new interests, formulas and strategies are emerging that condition the way in which content is created, produced and distributed (Telkmann, 2021;Doyle, 2016;Smith & Hendricks, 2010). Television series, in particular, are presented as the central element in the offer of SVOD platforms, so it could be said that the rise of the serialised fiction format has been decisive in the transition towards on-demand consumption, while other formats such as reality shows have gained great weight in conventional television (Villegas, 2018;Hidalgo-Marí et al., 2021). 

This paper includes research carried out from the perspective of content production that provides data on production companies, platforms and production strategies detected in the recent scenario of Spanish serialised fiction created specifically for SVOD. The study aims to establish a state of the art that goes a step further into the study of production and its different formulations as a determining element of the general offer of series on SVOD platforms.

Title: Radio’s Role in Digital Information Dissemination
Snippet: The findings reveal that Motion Radio adopts a selective content curation strategy, prioritizing informative, educational, and socially relevant programs over purely entertainment-oriented broadcasts. Podcast content is primarily derived from recorded on-air programs and repackaged for digital distribution, demonstrating an integrated production model in which existing broadcast workflows are optimized to serve dual platforms. This approach reflects organizational efficiency in the absence of a dedicated podcast team, while simultaneously presenting managerial challenges related to limited human resources and time constraints. 

Furthermore, podcasts are positioned as an extension of Motion Radio's institutional identity as an information-oriented broadcaster. Rather than functioning solely as archival storage, podcasts are strategically utilized to reach digitally oriented audience segments who may not regularly engage with traditional radio. Overall, the table highlights how podcasting operates as both a technological adaptation and a strategic communication response within Motion Radio's media convergence framework. The first finding indicates that the development of podcasts by Motion Radio is driven by the need to overcome the limitations of radio broadcasts, which are ephemeral and cannot be replayed. Informants emphasized that much informative content considered valuable for listeners may be missed if it is only broadcast live. Therefore, podcasts are utilized as a means to extend content accessibility, allowing audiences to listen to the content again at different times. 

The second finding relates to the podcast content curation strategy. Motion Radio does not upload all radio broadcast materials into podcast format; instead, it selectively curates specific content. Priority is given to informative, educational, and listener-relevant materials, such as topics on health, careers, public policy, and social issues. In contrast, light entertainment-oriented content tends not to be converted into podcasts, as it is considered to have limited long-term utility. 

The third finding shows that the primary source of Motion Radio's podcast content comes from live (on-air) broadcasts. Podcasts are not produced as entirely separate content, but rather as recordings and repackaged versions of talk shows or dialogues that have already been aired. This practice indicates that podcasts are positioned as an extension of radio broadcasts rather than as standalone media products. 

The fourth finding concerns the podcast production model implemented by Motion Radio. Podcast production is carried out in an integrated manner with radio broadcast production, without a dedicated podcast team.

Title: Streaming Queer Content: LGBTQ Media on BVOD and SVOD Services in Australia
Snippet: This extends to their BVOD services, which have unique exclusive digital content such as web series. Broadly, though, Australia's BVOD services contain content that is originally distributed elsewhere, and they employ strategies for discoverability that align with broadcast programing-that is, to maximize the audience. Although some BVOD services provide exclusive streaming content, their focus is generally on highlighting programing from the linear schedule. In contrast, as Lotz (2022) highlights, SVODs adopt different industrial practices as their value proposition is based on offering users access to a library of on-demand content. SVOD libraries typically contain licensed content and/or owned intellectual property, which can include bespoke content produced for the service and titles initially produced for other distribution contexts (Lotz 2022). SVODs differ from BVODs in that they aim to cultivate niche audiences, building and retain subscribers through personalized discoverability strategies (Khoo 2023) or expertly curating categories (Balanzategui and Lynch 2023). 

This article takes a broad approach to understand the inclusion of queer content in the streaming landscape in Australia, examining both BVOD and SVOD services. This is not to conflate the two models (and the finer variations within them) but to recognize that while BVOD and SVOD do differ, they collectively make up the experience of streaming video in Australia today. Moreover, in research on inclusion of diverse characters, they are often considered together (Screen Australia 2023). Though their processes are motivated by different means and shaped by different industrial forces, Australia's BVOD and SVOD services are similar in their employment of basic discoverability features. To this end, this article focuses on the mechanisms through which LGBTQ content is categorized, curated, and searchable (or not) on BVOD services from public service broadcasters ABC iView and SBS On Demand as well as commercial networks, 9Now, 7plus, and 10Play, local SVOD services Stan and Binge, and international SVOD services, Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video.

snippet.text:
This extends to their BVOD services, which have unique exclusive digital content such as web series. Broadly, though, Australia's BVOD services contain content that is originally distributed elsewhere, and they employ strategies for discoverability that align with broadcast programing-that is, to maximize the audience. Although some BVOD services provide exclusive streaming content, their focus is generally on highlighting programing from the linear schedule. In contrast, as Lotz (2022) highlights, SVODs adopt different industrial practices as their value proposition is based on offering users access to a library of on-demand content. SVOD libraries typically contain licensed content and/or owned intellectual property, which can include bespoke content produced for the service and titles initially produced for other distribution contexts (Lotz 2022). SVODs differ from BVODs in that they aim to cultivate niche audiences, building and retain subscribers through personalized discoverability strategies (Khoo 2023) or expertly curating categories (Balanzategui and Lynch 2023). 

This article takes a broad approach to understand the inclusion of queer content in the streaming landscape in Australia, examining both BVOD and SVOD services. This is not to conflate the two models (and the finer variations within them) but to recognize that while BVOD and SVOD do differ, they collectively make up the experience of streaming video in Australia today. Moreover, in research on inclusion of diverse characters, they are often considered together (Screen Australia 2023). Though their processes are motivated by different means and shaped by different industrial forces, Australia's BVOD and SVOD services are similar in their employment of basic discoverability features. To this end, this article focuses on the mechanisms through which LGBTQ content is categorized, curated, and searchable (or not) on BVOD services from public service broadcasters ABC iView and SBS On Demand as well as commercial networks, 9Now, 7plus, and 10Play, local SVOD services Stan and Binge, and international SVOD services, Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video.

documents.title: The production of Spanish fiction series for SVOD: evolution, trends and strategies
documents.snippet: The consolidation of digital television via subscription video on demand (SVOD) services has created an unprecedented increase in the consumption of serialised TV shows, which has had direct consequences on the content production sector. Faced with an increasingly demanding, hyperconnected and discerning audience and a supply of content never previously seen, television production and distribution strategies are involved in a process of change and adaptation. This paper seeks to analyse the production of Spanish television series created to be distributed on SVOD platforms. The aim is to know the role that production companies play in the creation of television series for SVOD so as to identify strategies and cooperative alliances between production companies and platforms and to detect possible patterns and trends in the operations of the audiovisual market. Using a mixed methodology that combines quantitative study with qualitative data analysis, the 88 Spanish TV series and miniseries that premiered on SVOD platforms from 2016 to 2021 are analysed, taking as a starting point the year in which these platforms began operating in Spain. The results confirm a trend towards cooperation between independent production companies and the platforms themselves, while no presence of in-house production is observed. Likewise, the atomisation of the role of production companies in the context of SVOD is shown, a phenomenon that already existed in generalist television production.

documents.title: Streaming Diversité: Exploring representations within French-language scripted series on Canadian SVOD services
documents.snippet:
In the era of SVOD services, original content is key. Historically, streaming services' catalogs were predominantly comprised of licensed programs. However, with the proliferation of platforms, SVOD services started prioritizing original content (Lotz, 2022;Lotz and Lobato, 2023). Focusing on 'original content' is especially instructive as it sheds light on a streaming service's curatorial and programming strategies. It offers insights into a platform's content development ethosessentially, the brand identity it endeavors to forge and the narrative trends it deems most compelling. As Lotz argues: 'Distinguishing bespoke content developed specifically for the SVOD is important because services are able to deploy explicit content strategies through these titles'. (2022: 9) Furthermore, because of the specific affordances of internet distribution (Lotz, 2017;Lotz and Lobato, 2023), studying original productions is particularly instrumental in understanding the 'new kinds of creative possibilities for creators […], [and] modes of storytelling the affordances of SVOD allow' (Lotz and Lobato, 2023: 4). 

Yet, the concept of 'original content', often ubiquitously deployed within the media industry, eludes a simplistic definition and warrants further elucidation. As Matthew Ball (2018) contends: '"Original" isn't a technical definition but a marketing one. And thus not only is the definition of "Original" vague, it also differs from network to network'. In academic circles, 'original content' is broadly classified into four distinct categories (Afilipoaie et al., 2021;Ball 2018) : (1) developed originals, that is, bespoke content that is commissioned and produced directly for a streaming service; (2) acquired originals, i.e., content that is purchased after production or to resume production; (3) co-productions between a streaming service and a national broadcaster; and (4) licensed originals, which refer to works not initially made for a streaming service but that have been granted exclusive online distribution rights.

documents.title: The production of Spanish fiction series for SVOD: evolution, trends and strategies
documents.snippet:
The arrival of Netflix in 2015, together with the first á la carte actions of Movistar+, marked the beginning of a new television era in Spain orientated towards on-demand consumption. A year later, HBO and Amazon Prime Video, as well as the rest of the platforms that have successively joined the on-demand service, ended up altering both the way of consuming television and the usual programming process and, by extension, the production of television content. The flow TV, or planned flow, which Raymond Williams (1974) defined as the strategy based on the programming blocks of television channels whose intention was to retain and build audience loyalty, loses its meaning in the context of on-demand television, in which big data and personalisation algorithms are the only valid flows for building loyalty, recommending or making attractive content visible to digital audiences (Heredia-Ruiz, Quirós-Ramírez & Quiceno-Castañeda, 2021). Accordingly, in recent years the planned flow that had characterised television strategy almost from its origins has been replaced by the offer of on-demand content, modifying the strategic positioning of the different multimedia groups, television channels, production companies and, of course, consumers themselves. 

In a changing television scenario, in which video on demand appears to lead the race for content, new interests, formulas and strategies are emerging that condition the way in which content is created, produced and distributed (Telkmann, 2021;Doyle, 2016;Smith & Hendricks, 2010). Television series, in particular, are presented as the central element in the offer of SVOD platforms, so it could be said that the rise of the serialised fiction format has been decisive in the transition towards on-demand consumption, while other formats such as reality shows have gained great weight in conventional television (Villegas, 2018;Hidalgo-Marí et al., 2021). 

This paper includes research carried out from the perspective of content production that provides data on production companies, platforms and production strategies detected in the recent scenario of Spanish serialised fiction created specifically for SVOD. The study aims to establish a state of the art that goes a step further into the study of production and its different formulations as a determining element of the general offer of series on SVOD platforms.

Title: The Influence of Perceived Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Personalization on Subscription Video on Demand Continuance Intentions
Snippet: The result is in line with the previous research [26,[69][70][71][72]87]. However, the result is not following other previous research [88]. Personalization does not affect continuance intention directly. However, it indirectly affects continuance intention through the mediation of habit. Based on the interview, it is identified that eight out of ten interviewees feel that personalization is one of the features in Netflix that makes them satisfied and want to reuse the service ("Content, price, application's UI/UX, good recommendations" -Interviewee 1. "Recommendations are really good, according to the genre" -Interviewee 2. "I really like the recommendation system" -Interviewee 3. "The feature of a movie recommendation makes me satisfied" -Interviewee 5. "Recommendations on Netflix are one of the features that make me like using Netflix" -Interviewee 6. "Recommendation of movies according to your wishes makes it more time-saving to look for movies" -Interviewee 7. "One of the features that make you feel at home is movie recommendations according to your preferences" -Interviewee 9. "One of the factors that makes you satisfied is the recommendation of films on Netflix that can show films according to your interests" -Interviewee 10). Personalization is a relevant determinant of the use of a service and significantly impacts the user's intention to continue using the service [89]. The results of the questionnaire data show that 75.36% of respondents use Netflix's SVoD service more than three times a week. When they feel that an SVoD service can provide services according to their preferences, they will be more inclined to continue to reuse the SVoD service. 

Finally, the research contributes to literature review that presents the context of SVoD, especially in Indonesia. The findings provide an extension of previous research on SVoD [3,32], ISS model [31,42,58,90], and technologies that implement personalization [25,26,69,70,87]. The results also indicate that the information quality does not affect satisfaction [76,78,84].

Title: Datacasting: TikTok’s Algorithmic Flow as Televisual Experience
Snippet: By simplifying the recommendation process by implementing automated algorithmic feeds, social media platforms such as the aforementioned have managed to attract more and more viewers throughout the years, with a study conducted by Deloitte in 2023 confirming that people belonging to Generation Z (1997)(1998)(1999)(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009) have started preferring video content available on social media to traditional television (Westcott  et al., 2023). One of the hypothesised reasons is the ease with which it is possible to find enjoyable content on social media, compared to the choice overload (cf. Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, 2015, p. 2) faced by users on traditional subscription video on demand (SVOD) services. 

As we have seen, personalisation is at the centre of contemporary flow experiences, in that most platforms and services that currently offer audiovisual content are algorithm-based. What this entails is that home pages within streaming services are built according to users' algorithmic identities (Cheney-Lippold, 2011), and that these services act as gatekeepers, only showing subscribers the content they deem appropriate (Van Esler, 2021). In analysing SVOD platforms, Cox highlighted the importance of focusing on two distinct aspects of the services: televisible elements, which refer to visual elements within the interface, and invisual elements, algorithms, and softwares that influence the way in which users interact with the service (2018). The former become fundamental in shaping user experience on the platform: As highlighted by Johnson (2019), SVOD services provide users with (seemingly) infinite rows of content, which provide the feeling of choosing from an ample catalogue, although the platform algorithms are merely offering "more of the same" (Lüders & Shanke Sundet, 2022). The latter, on the other hand, are one of the key components of datacasting experiences, in that they are crucial in ensuring that the personalisation that services enact is effective.

Title: When the Known Well May Sell
Snippet: While Streaming Video on Demand (SVOD) consumers may express a desire for unlimited new and novel choices, excess choice can cause anxiety and choice overload. Further, familiarity can also influence perceptions of available choices. Addressing a gap in the literature on familiarity’s interaction with choice numeracy in an SVOD recommendation environment, this 2x2 experiment examines effects of choice-set size of TV sitcoms on potential use/perceptions of SVOD platforms and to what extent familiarity with the choices interacts with those perceptions through examining differences and interactions between small vs large choice sets, and familiar vs non-familiar shows. Familiarity tends to override potential choice overload effects and non-familiarity tends to exacerbate negative effects associated with too much choice, which has implications for purveyors of not only SVOD systems but other digital applications with similar recommendation systems, such as music streaming and podcasts, to emphasise choices that are likely to have familiarity to consumers, especially when interfaces themselves may be unfamiliar.

Title: The Influence of Perceived Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Personalization on Subscription Video on Demand Continuance Intentions
Snippet: The research aims to analyze the factors influencing the intention to continue using SVoD with Netflix as the case study. The research identifies that SVoD service quality affects the confirmation of the user's initial expectations for the service. The quality of the SVoD system also influences the perceived usefulness of SVoD. Furthermore, confirmation of users' initial expectations for SVoD affects users' perceived usefulness and satisfaction with SVoD services. Finally, the intention to continue using SVoD is influenced by the personalization of content, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction with SVoD services. 

Nevertheless, the research has a limitation that the respondents are dominated by an age range of 17-25 years. Hence, they do not represent respondents in all age ranges. Most of the respondent's domicile is from the Greater Jakarta area, and they do not represent all SVoD service users in Indonesia. Lastly, the research only focuses on one type of SVoD, namely Netflix. Future research can expand respondents in terms of age, area of residence, and type of SVoD. Further research can also consider perceived price and content diversity to enrich the theory of the effect of user satisfaction on SVoD or similar services.

Title: A Comprehensive Review on Video Recommendation System: Models, Challenges, and Applications
Snippet: The recommendation system is a skilled system to recognize the preferences, preceding decisions, and distinctiveness of people's choices, and gathering data regarding their product use is very interactive. These comprise impressions, clicks, likes, and purchases. Because recommendation systems can predict consumer interests and desires on an extremely personalized level, they are preferred by content and product providers. Recommendation systems can attract consumers to just about any product or service that makes them interesting from books to videos to health classes to clothing. Historically, the Netflix recommendation system has encountered issues in accurately predicting user ratings. Consumer research suggests that many Netflix. Members lose interest after searching for only 60-90 seconds, typically viewing just 10 to 20 titles across two screens. To address these problems, Netflix has developed various strategies to enhance user engagement and maintain interest. Nowadays, Netflix recommendation systems use algorithms to predict and suggest items based on user preferences and interactions with various platforms [32]. Internet TV is the user's first choice compared to cable and broadcast. This flexibility is because of the vast use of the internet the user can decide how, where, when, and what to watch their preferred video [33]. 

Netflix hosted a renowned competition aimed at refining its recommendation system through collaborative filtering algorithms. This competition, launched on October 6th, 2006 by Netflix, Inc., presented a significant challenge to Netflix's existing recommendation system, known as Cinematch [34]. Termed the Netflix Prize [35][36], it aimed to achieve superior prediction accuracy compared to Cinematch. The prize offered by Netflix, a total amount of 1 million dollars, was the inspiration behind its name [37], and it was awarded to the team that could develop a specified recommendation system [38]. The primary objective of the Netflix Prize was to improve the movie recommendation system [39] by more accurately predicting users' preferences and enhancing the overall user experience [40]. The Netflix Prize operated by providing participants with a dataset consisting of movie ratings from 100 million ratings by 480,000 users across nearly 18,000 movies, contributed by anonymous users. Participants were tasked with predicting how users would rate movies that had not yet seen, thereby developing recommendation algorithms. Over 50,000 participants from 186 countries took part in this competition, forming approximately 40,000 teams.

Personalization is a relevant determinant of the use of a service and significantly impacts the user's intention to continue using the service [89]. The results of the questionnaire data show that 75.36% of respondents use Netflix's SVoD service more than three times a week. When they feel that an SVoD service can provide services according to their preferences, they will be more inclined to continue to reuse the SVoD service. 

Finally, the research contributes to literature review that presents the context of SVoD, especially in Indonesia. The findings provide an extension of previous research on SVoD [3,32], ISS model [31,42,58,90], and technologies that implement personalization [25,26,69,70,87]. The results also indicate that the information quality does not affect satisfaction [76,78,84].

documents.title: Datacasting: TikTok’s Algorithmic Flow as Televisual Experience
documents.snippet:
By simplifying the recommendation process by implementing automated algorithmic feeds, social media platforms such as the aforementioned have managed to attract more and more viewers throughout the years, with a study conducted by Deloitte in 2023 confirming that people belonging to Generation Z (1997)(1998)(1999)(2000)(2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009) have started preferring video content available on social media to traditional television (Westcott  et al., 2023). One of the hypothesised reasons is the ease with which it is possible to find enjoyable content on social media, compared to the choice overload (cf. Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, 2015, p. 2) faced by users on traditional subscription video on demand (SVOD) services. 

As we have seen, personalisation is at the centre of contemporary flow experiences, in that most platforms and services that currently offer audiovisual content are algorithm-based. What this entails is that home pages within streaming services are built according to users' algorithmic identities (Cheney-Lippold, 2011), and that these services act as gatekeepers, only showing subscribers the content they deem appropriate (Van Esler, 2021). In analysing SVOD platforms, Cox highlighted the importance of focusing on two distinct aspects of the services: televisible elements, which refer to visual elements within the interface, and invisual elements, algorithms, and softwares that influence the way in which users interact with the service (2018). The former become fundamental in shaping user experience on the platform: As highlighted by Johnson (2019), SVOD services provide users with (seemingly) infinite rows of content, which provide the feeling of choosing from an ample catalogue, although the platform algorithms are merely offering "more of the same" (Lüders & Shanke Sundet, 2022). The latter, on the other hand, are one of the key components of datacasting experiences, in that they are crucial in ensuring that the personalisation that services enact is effective.

documents.title: When the Known Well May Sell
documents.snippet: While Streaming Video on Demand (SVOD) consumers may express a desire for unlimited new and novel choices, excess choice can cause anxiety and choice overload. Further, familiarity can also influence perceptions of available choices. Addressing a gap in the literature on familiarity’s interaction with choice numeracy in an SVOD recommendation environment, this 2x2 experiment examines effects of choice-set size of TV sitcoms on potential use/perceptions of SVOD platforms and to what extent familiarity with the choices interacts with those perceptions through examining differences and interactions between small vs large choice sets, and familiar vs non-familiar shows. Familiarity tends to override potential choice overload effects and non-familiarity tends to exacerbate negative effects associated with too much choice, which has implications for purveyors of not only SVOD systems but other digital applications with similar recommendation systems, such as music streaming and podcasts, to emphasise choices that are likely to have familiarity to consumers, especially when interfaces themselves may be unfamiliar.

documents.title: The Influence of Perceived Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Personalization on Subscription Video on Demand Continuance Intentions
documents.snippet:
The research aims to analyze the factors influencing the intention to continue using SVoD with Netflix as the case study. The research identifies that SVoD service quality affects the confirmation of the user's initial expectations for the service. The quality of the SVoD system also influences the perceived usefulness of SVoD. Furthermore, confirmation of users' initial expectations for SVoD affects users' perceived usefulness and satisfaction with SVoD services. Finally, the intention to continue using SVoD is influenced by the personalization of content, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction with SVoD services. 

Nevertheless, the research has a limitation that the respondents are dominated by an age range of 17-25 years. Hence, they do not represent respondents in all age ranges. Most of the respondent's domicile is from the Greater Jakarta area, and they do not represent all SVoD service users in Indonesia. Lastly, the research only focuses on one type of SVoD, namely Netflix. Future research can expand respondents in terms of age, area of residence, and type of SVoD. Further research can also consider perceived price and content diversity to enrich the theory of the effect of user satisfaction on SVoD or similar services.

documents.title: A Comprehensive Review on Video Recommendation System: Models, Challenges, and Applications
documents.snippet:
The recommendation system is a skilled system to recognize the preferences, preceding decisions, and distinctiveness of people's choices, and gathering data regarding their product use is very interactive. These comprise impressions, clicks, likes, and purchases. Because recommendation systems can predict consumer interests and desires on an extremely personalized level, they are preferred by content and product providers. Recommendation systems can attract consumers to just about any product or service that makes them interesting from books to videos to health classes to clothing. Historically, the Netflix recommendation system has encountered issues in accurately predicting user ratings. Consumer research suggests that many Netflix. Members lose interest after searching for only 60-90 seconds, typically viewing just 10 to 20 titles across two screens. To address these problems, Netflix has developed various strategies to enhance user engagement and maintain interest. Nowadays, Netflix recommendation systems use algorithms to predict and suggest items based on user preferences and interactions with various platforms [32]. Internet TV is the user's first choice compared to cable and broadcast. This flexibility is because of the vast use of the internet the user can decide how, where, when, and what to watch their preferred video [33]. 

Netflix hosted a renowned competition aimed at refining its recommendation system through collaborative filtering algorithms. This competition, launched on October 6th, 2006 by Netflix, Inc., presented a significant challenge to Netflix's existing recommendation system, known as Cinematch [34]. Termed the Netflix Prize [35][36], it aimed to achieve superior prediction accuracy compared to Cinematch. The prize offered by Netflix, a total amount of 1 million dollars, was the inspiration behind its name [37], and it was awarded to the team that could develop a specified recommendation system [38]. The primary objective of the Netflix Prize was to improve the movie recommendation system [39] by more accurately predicting users' preferences and enhancing the overall user experience [40]. The Netflix Prize operated by providing participants with a dataset consisting of movie ratings from 100 million ratings by 480,000 users across nearly 18,000 movies, contributed by anonymous users. Participants were tasked with predicting how users would rate movies that had not yet seen, thereby developing recommendation algorithms. Over 50,000 participants from 186 countries took part in this competition, forming approximately 40,000 teams.

Title: The show must go on(line): the impact of content and system quality on the usage of television streaming content libraries
Snippet: The main aim of this paper is to analyze the influencing factors of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes of content library usage.Content libraries (sometimes also called media libraries, Gutzeit et al., 2021) can be defined as closed television station portals structured like libraries with professionally produced (long-format) content; the majority of content is repurposed from the linear television programming schedule (Lobato, 2019;Lotz, 2017).Such content libraries have become a global phenomenon.In countries such as the UK, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Argentina, or Japan, television broadcasters complement their linear offerings via Internet Protocol-distributed, advertising-financed and/or subscription-based content libraries (see examples in Table A1 in the Appendix).These offerings have become a relevant part of the streaming video competition landscape.Hulu, which started by curating the catch-up offerings of U.S. television channels, counts among the most popular SVoD providers, with 28% of U.S. adults tuning in at least every week (Morning Consult, 2022).

In the European context, several television groups have complemented their catch-up content libraries with original content, establishing those offers as part of the streaming consumption mix.Our research focuses on the German media market, one of the largest markets for SVoD in the world (Rahe et al., 2021).The German media system is characterized by strong competition between private and public service broadcasters, which extends to the SVoD market, with both groups attracting substantial usage of their content library offerings (ARD/ZDF Forschungskommission, 2023).Also, private and public groups both invest substantial sums in content production and content libraries (ARD, 2023;Meier, 2023), making these well-developed offerings a suitable object of investigation.As a result, content library usage is well established: 39% of Germans use content libraries on a daily or weekly basis (ARD/ZDF Forschungskommission, 2023; Schauerte et al., 2021).

Title: New audience dimensions in streaming platforms: the second life of Money heist on Netflix as a case study
Snippet: Based on the analysis, we conclude that a revised concept of audience in the context of SVOD should consider a number of aspects: -It is constructed from an enormous volume of data whose main characteristic is its fragmentation (fragmented audience). -Audience research in this context involves interpreting and assigning a value to each new audience dimension arising from online consumption (weighted audience) and not just accumulating data. -The volatility inherent in these platform audiences, jumping easily between content and services -a volatile or 'gaseous' audience, using the term in Callejo-Gallego (2019)-, suggests that weight should be given to what is chosen and the quality of such choices, thereby producing new audience dimensions based on the connection established with content (adhered audience).

Given this revised concept of SVOD audience (fragmented, weighted, volatile and adhered), this study concludes that new dimensions above and beyond data provided by TAMs should be included. Such new dimensions are based on the premise that the value of the audience is not just its size, but also its engagement (users' involvement with content) and its depth of attention (audience density, to use Netflix's term). In assigning value to audience attention, the methodology used by Parrot Analytics, which takes us into the field of big data, opens up an interesting line of research: varying the weighting based on users' level of effort, both internally (frequency, intensity and repeat viewing) and externally (posts on social media, information searches in Google, illegal downloads).

Title: The production of Spanish fiction series for SVOD: evolution, trends and strategies
Snippet: The consolidation of digital television via subscription video on demand (SVOD) services has created an unprecedented increase in the consumption of serialised TV shows, which has had direct consequences on the content production sector. Faced with an increasingly demanding, hyperconnected and discerning audience and a supply of content never previously seen, television production and distribution strategies are involved in a process of change and adaptation. This paper seeks to analyse the production of Spanish television series created to be distributed on SVOD platforms. The aim is to know the role that production companies play in the creation of television series for SVOD so as to identify strategies and cooperative alliances between production companies and platforms and to detect possible patterns and trends in the operations of the audiovisual market. Using a mixed methodology that combines quantitative study with qualitative data analysis, the 88 Spanish TV series and miniseries that premiered on SVOD platforms from 2016 to 2021 are analysed, taking as a starting point the year in which these platforms began operating in Spain. The results confirm a trend towards cooperation between independent production companies and the platforms themselves, while no presence of in-house production is observed. Likewise, the atomisation of the role of production companies in the context of SVOD is shown, a phenomenon that already existed in generalist television production.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer clearly identifies multiple SVOD practices that traditional broadcasters have NOT adopted: (1) algorithmic personalization and recommendation systems as central loyalty/development engines, (2) originals-led brand building with independent producers and platformized workflows, (3) data-driven attention-weighted metrics (engagement over TAMs), (4) micro-operations without commercial breaks, (5) first-party OTT app control with direct-to-consumer branding, and (6) recommendation-driven libraries (vs. BVOD mirroring of linear schedules). For each non-adoption, the answer provides evidence-based reasoning that goes beyond 'no papers mention it': it cites structural constraints including advertiser dependence and commercial break protection [1], legacy linear scheduling norms and 'flow TV' identity [1], organizational path dependence in production models [1], infrastructure and policy gaps [12], fragmented rights and carriage regimes [11], and risk aversion around brand dilution [2]. The answer does not claim broadcasters have adopted these practices—indeed, it explicitly contrasts SVOD strategies with broadcaster behavior (e.g., BVOD services 'highlight linear programming' vs. SVOD personalization [10], broadcasters 'repurpose on-air content' rather than standalone originals [7]). The cited sources support rather than contradict the non-adoption claims.
other_issues: The answer is extremely verbose and repetitive, with significant overlap between the 'Production strategies' and 'Distribution strategies' sections—many points (e.g., algorithmic personalization, originals, micro-ops) are rehashed multiple times with similar citations.
The summary at the beginning is dense and difficult to parse, mixing multiple claims without clear prioritization or structure.

Some citations are tangential: [7] (Motion Radio podcasts) and [12] (AI in Akwa Ibom radio) are drawn from niche, non-SVOD/broadcaster contexts and feel forced into the argument rather than directly illuminating broadcaster-SVOD strategic divergence.
The 'Implications and outlook' section adds little new information and largely repeats earlier points, contributing to the overall length without substantive insight.

Minor: The phrase 'micro-operations without commercial breaks' is somewhat jargony and not clearly defined; the answer conflates 'no commercial breaks' with 'micro-ops' and 'binge pacing' in ways that may confuse readers unfamiliar with the domain.
judgment.summary: The answer satisfies the verification criterion by naming multiple specific SVOD practices not adopted by broadcasters and providing evidence-based structural/strategic reasoning (advertiser dependence, legacy scheduling, infrastructure gaps, regulatory constraints) rather than absence-of-mention. However, the answer is excessively long, repetitive, and structurally disorganized, with some tangential citations that weaken its focus. Future iterations should prioritize clarity, concision, and relevance of evidence.
