attempts.answer:
Summary
Traditional broadcasters’ early responses to SVOD (2010–2015)—mixing mimicry (multiscreen apps and “catch‑up”), strategic collaboration (platform joint ventures and paid partnerships), and resistance (bundle defense and pricing hold‑ups)—created organizational and technological lock‑in that now limits competitive options. Evidence spans organizational path dependencies (bureaucracy and linear production routines), governance overreach that entrenches legacy control, late and bundle‑tied integrations with SVODs, and market‑level network effects that make exit costly. Alternative early choices—earlier standalone SVOD launches, neutral platform governance, studio‑direct distribution, ad‑supported experimentation, and modernized conditional access/API ecosystems—would have reduced lock‑in and positioned incumbents better, though they carry their own trade‑offs.

Organizational lock‑in: routines, governance, and delayed capability building
- Broadcasters and public service broadcasters gravitated toward “mimicry” and “strategic collaboration” with SVODs rather than systematic reinvention of production and distribution logic, adopting streaming production culture and partnerships to appear adaptive while facing concerns over “platformisation” that erode institutional roles and funding stability <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Traditional broadcasters adopted strategic responses to SVODs including mimicry and strategic collaboration, raising concerns about platformisation and the erosion of public service roles and funding</cite>. 
- Organizational architectures built for continuous linear production and centralized hierarchies (e.g., in‑house broadcasters) are structurally conservative: continuous production lines and bureaucracies blunt innovation incentives, making flexible specialization for digital demand harder to embed without long‑run capability lock‑in <cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Introducing innovation is difficult in organizations where continuous production is paramount, with bureaucracies focused on a continuous stream of programmes, impeding change toward demand-driven digital models</cite>. 
- Governance overreach can entrench lock‑in: Disney’s early investment in Hulu simultaneously deepened control via board dominance and exclusive licensing that shielded legacy networks, signaling that SVOD access would be mediated by traditional TV power, with popular Disney hits initially withheld from Hulu to assert leverage <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s board appointments and exclusive licensing extended legacy control over Hulu, with popular Disney programming initially unavailable on Hulu to signal traditional TV powers would dictate content available to SVOD users</cite>. 
- Market‑level network effects and pricing power reinforce incumbents’ platforms: SVODs altered monetization formats and unbundled subscriptions, but pay‑TV operators’ historical bundles and relationships created path dependencies; when pressure mounted, late deals (e.g., Comcast–Netflix in 2016; Sky–Netflix in 2018; Foxtel price cuts in 2014) were driven by bundle defense and pricing competition, underscoring late, reactive integration with legacy set‑top boxes and pay‑TV pricing rather than first‑party OTT refactoring <cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundled subscriptions and simplified contracts relative to pay-TV, bringing AVoD to the forefront and making SVOD less tightly coupled to cable/satellite infrastructure than legacy pay-per-view</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-4">Comcast and Netflix struck a deal in July 2016 to include Netflix in the Comcast X1 set-top box; Sky partnered with Netflix in 2018 to retain customers; Foxtel halved basic subscription pricing months before Netflix’s arrival</cite>. 
- Consumer multi‑homing and platform pricing policies create sticky ecosystems: as SVODs expand, users subscribe to multiple platforms and legacy media “cord‑couple” to hybrid bundles; anti‑sharing enforcement increases revenue but risks cancellations, illustrating how pricing and access control bind users and firms into overlapping networks—raising exit and platform‑switching costs <cite id="1e32db7b-3">Multi-homing is rising, with many subscribing to multiple SVODs; SVOD operators are adopting password-sharing restrictions to lock in users, though increased costs can spur cancellations</cite><cite id="c6225eae-1">Providers such as Netflix, Disney, and Hulu eliminated password sharing to enhance profitability, but the policy trade-offs raise subscription cancellation risks and uncertainty about long-run viability</cite>.

Technological lock‑in: delivery pipelines, DRM, and late platform integration
- Pay‑TV operators’ reliance on proprietary set‑top environments and bundled pricing delayed true OTT refactoring: forced integrations like Netflix in X1 and Sky’s late partnerships embedded SVOD into legacy interfaces, preserving linear bundling economics and data silos, which restricts agile, consumer‑first experimentation and data‑driven personalization that scale with pure SVODs <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late partnerships (Comcast–Netflix, Sky–Netflix) and Foxtel price cuts were responses to cord-cutting pressures, embedding SVOD into legacy set-top boxes and pay-TV pricing structures</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD typically unbundles to broadband/telephony and can be terminated at short notice, contrasting with pay-TV’s bundled infrastructure and complex legacy contracts</cite>. 
- Governance‑by‑conglomerate ownership and board control in early Hulu deepened platform coupling to legacy scheduling and advertising logics; content exclusivity and gatekeeping signaled that SVOD access remains a lever of traditional power, discouraging neutral, open platform approaches that could have reduced lock‑in <cite id="c6225eae-0">Hulu’s board included top Disney/NBC/News Corp executives, and Disney withheld popular programming to demonstrate traditional television powers would dictate Hulu’s content</cite>. 
- Market structure and data/monetization shifts are locked in by two‑sided platform designs: AVoD’s rise foregrounded advertising as a core revenue stream; SVOD’s subscription unbundling and flexible packaging altered legacy relationships with advertisers and distributors, but incumbents’ late moves to integrate SVODs into existing ad systems and distribution channels constrained experimentation with pure ad‑supported and data‑native models <cite id="1e32db7b-1">Advertising became a key revenue stream in the streaming era; SVOD’s subscription unbundling and simpler contracts contrasted with legacy pay-TV and PPV models</cite>. 
- Platformization and content control raise institutional risks: as broadcasters “build like platforms” via partnerships and in‑house apps, they risk ceding distribution power to platforms while retaining content control, creating dependency on platform gateways and pricing policies that limit autonomy and responsiveness <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Mimicking SVOD strategies and engaging in strategic collaborations raised concerns about platformisation of culture and the erosion of public service broadcasters’ roles</cite>.

Evidence that alternative early choices would have positioned incumbents better
- Earlier, more aggressive standalone SVOD entry by studios and networks: Disney’s later success with Disney+ and its bundled acceleration (100 million subscribers in 16 months) relied on a direct consumer stack that only emerged after sustained linear losses; had Disney earlier prioritized studio‑direct SVOD alongside linear networks, it would have de‑coupled distribution faster and reduced reliance on cash flows from theme parks and linear ads, though with similar content‑control trade‑offs <cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s direct-to-consumer streaming segment grew to $20.5B in FY2023 but reported aggregate streaming losses of $4.2B, highlighting financial dependence on traditional segments even as streaming accelerates</cite><cite id="c6225eae-2">Disney’s 2019 Disney+ launch into a consolidating SVOD market illustrates high sector concentration and the premium on global brands, supporting earlier direct SVOD positioning as a strategic lever</cite>. 
- Neutral platform governance and open ecosystems: European legacy players’ joint domestic platform (Streamz) shows that early collaboration to emulate core advantages of global platforms is possible but constrained by small‑market politics and capital, underscoring how governance design and funding structures can either reduce or deepen lock‑in; neutral, open APIs and de‑verticalized access would have mitigated proprietary lock‑in with Netflix/Disney and preserved competition <cite id="c6225eae-4">Legacy media collaboration on a domestic SVOD (Streamz) illustrates how policy-driven collaboration can create a joint venture but faces significant challenges in a highly competitive market, limiting the platform’s ability to stand a chance</cite>. 
- Pay‑TV modernization and MVPD adaptation: early investment in conditional‑access refactoring, neutral MVPD APIs, and data/identity layers would have enabled smoother OTT aggregation and multi‑home support rather than forcing late integrations like Netflix in X1/Sky, which preserved linear bundles and slowed personalized, cross‑screen experiences <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Comcast’s inclusion of Netflix in X1 and Sky’s partnership with Netflix reflect late-stage integrations driven by bundle protection and pricing competition</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD’s unbundling and termination flexibility contrast with legacy pay-TV’s bundled infrastructure, suggesting earlier modernization would reduce coupling</cite>. 
- Studio‑direct consumer stacks and ad‑supported experimentation: Disney’s Premier Access hybrid model highlighted tensions between digital innovation and legacy theatrical partners; earlier, studio‑centric direct-to-consumer launch and ad‑supported SVOD experimentation would have reduced dependence on theatrical gatekeepers and diversified monetization, though with profitability risks and distribution conflicts <cite id="c6225eae-3">Hybrid release strategies correlated with a 57% decline in per-screen revenue for Disney films in H2 2021, and Premier Access was discontinued in 2022, revealing tensions between digital innovation and legacy exhibition</cite>. 
- Consumer‑first pricing and access models: early adoption of flexible, multi‑home pricing and password‑sharing policies that balance retention and revenue (instead of heavy anti‑sharing) can lock users into bundles without mass churn, while late anti‑sharing shocks raise cancellation risk; learning from Netflix’s mixed outcomes, incumbents could have blended ad‑supported tiers and subsidized bundles to reduce lock‑in costs for consumers <cite id="1e32db7b-3">SVOD providers’ elimination of password sharing increased revenue but raised cancellation risks, showing policy trade-offs in locking in multi-homing users</cite><cite id="c6225eae-1">Anti-sharing policies can strengthen user lock-in but may undermine longevity, suggesting diversified pricing strategies to retain multi-homers</cite>. 
- Content strategy choices: early exclusives to attract subscribers (as Netflix built originals) versus late exclusives can create different platform power; Disney’s strategic withholding and gatekeeping in Hulu signaled traditional control and slowed balanced market competition, whereas earlier, reciprocal access and cross‑platform originals would have de‑risked user acquisition and reduced lock‑in <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s early Hulu deal withheld popular programming and emphasized board control, signaling that SVOD content access would be dictated by traditional TV powers</cite>. 
- Regional collaborations and distribution parity: early European alliances (e.g., Sky/Canal+/Netflix deals) show incumbents could have used joint ventures to grant parity of access across legacy networks, preventing single‑source dependence and creating competitive internal platforms; however, small‑market cases like Belgium’s Streamz demonstrate funding and policy constraints that still limit alternatives <cite id="c6225eae-4">Belgian legacy players’ joint venture (Streamz) shows policy-driven collaboration can create domestic platforms but faces significant market challenges in standing against global competitors</cite>. 

Mechanisms that limit options and suggest lock‑in
- Governance and control: Conglomerate ownership and board capture in early SVODs locked decision rights in legacy divisions, aligning platform strategy to preserve linear ad sales and bundling rather than consumer‑centered OTT, creating durable path dependence <cite id="c6225eae-0">Hulu’s board included top executives from NBCUniversal, News Corp, and Disney, with Disney withholding popular programming to assert control</cite>. 
- Network effects and two‑sided markets: SVOD’s unbundling and AVoD/FAST hybrids reframed audience and ad monetization; incumbents’ late integration deepened two‑sided dependencies with distributors and advertisers, while platform network effects bind users across overlapping SVODs and legacy bundles, raising switching costs <cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundling and AVoD’s rise reframed monetization; SVOD’s simpler unbundling contrasts with pay-TV’s complex legacy contracts</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-3">Rising multi-homing and platform pricing policies illustrate how lock-in operates across overlapping SVOD ecosystems</cite>. 
- Consumer behavior and pricing: The rise of multi‑homing and the sensitivity of SVOD churn to pricing and access policies mean incumbents must diversify and align pricing across linear and digital, or risk binding users into costly anti‑sharing regimes that backfire <cite id="1e32db7b-3">U.S. and German consumers subscribe to multiple SVODs on the rise; anti-sharing policies can raise revenue but trigger cancellations</cite>. 
- Organizational inertia: Continuous linear production and bureaucratic structures impede rapid reorientation toward demand‑driven, multiscreen production and data‑native operations, entrenching technological and organizational lock‑in <cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Organizations built for continuous linear production develop bureaucracies that impede innovation and flexible specialization for digital demand</cite>. 

What would have been better early choices and their trade‑offs
- Build neutral, open consumer platforms: Early MVPD‑neutral APIs, conditional‑access decoupling, and open identity/data layers would have allowed aggregation across legacy and SVOD catalogs without embedding content in proprietary set‑top gateways, improving user experience and retention while preserving competition; however, short‑term revenue synergies with SVOD licensors and bundle defenses made such openness politically and financially difficult <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late integrations like Netflix in X1 and Sky’s deals reflected bundle defense; earlier neutral APIs would have reduced gateway lock-in</cite>. 
- Studio‑centric direct distribution: Earlier Disney/Time‑Warner/CBS studio‑direct SVOD (e.g., branded tiers) would have accelerated acquisition and diversified revenue beyond linear ads; Disney’s experience shows rapid growth but persistent losses and conflicts with legacy exhibition, underscoring the need to balance near‑term profitability with long‑run platform investment and content‑studio relations <cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s streaming segment grew to $20.5B but reported $4.2B aggregate losses in FY2023, revealing the trade-off between growth and profitability in a DCI-dependent model</cite>. 
- Ad‑supported experimentation and diversified pricing: Early ad‑supported SVOD tiers and family‑shared plans to capture multi‑homing behavior would have reduced per‑user costs and dependence on paid password sharing; evidence shows anti‑sharing can raise revenue but also increase churn, so earlier diversified pricing would have balanced retention and monetization <cite id="1e32db7b-3">Multi-homing users increasingly subscribe to multiple SVODs; diversified pricing is needed to lock in users while mitigating the negative effects of anti-sharing policies</cite>. 
- Governance that de‑verticalizes platform control: Avoiding board capture and exclusive licensing that prioritize legacy gateways would have enabled more balanced access and faster data/monetization innovation; Disney’s early Hulu governance illustrates the opposite—content gatekeeping and board dominance that slowed parity and reinforced linear control <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s governance and exclusivity in Hulu signaled that SVOD access would be dictated by traditional TV powers</cite>. 
- Regional alliances with parity: Early European alliances (e.g., Sky/Canal+/Netflix) that grant equal access across legacy platforms and domestic SVODs could prevent single‑source dependence and foster competitive internal platforms; the Belgian Streamz case shows that while such choices are possible, funding, market size, and policy constraints limit scalability <cite id="c6225eae-4">Legacy players’ collaboration on Streamz shows policy and market constraints make profitable parity platforms hard to scale in small markets</cite>. 

Conclusion
The initial strategic responses of traditional broadcasters—mimicry, collaboration, and bundle‑defense—locked them into hybrid organizational and technological architectures that privilege legacy gateways and governance over consumer‑first platform design. Evidence from Disney/Hulu governance, late pay‑TV integrations with Netflix, organizational production bureaucracies, and market‑level network effects shows durable lock‑in in delivery pipelines, pricing, and content control. Alternative early choices—neutral MVPD platforms and APIs, studio‑direct SVOD launches with diversified pricing, ad‑supported experimentation, and de‑verticalized governance—would have reduced lock‑in, improved competitive positioning, and aligned incentives to monetize multi‑homing users; however, incumbents faced strong internal and external path dependencies that favored short‑term bundle preservation over long‑term platform freedom, producing the hybrid models we see today with both growth and persistent profitability headwinds <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Mimicry and collaboration with SVODs raised platformisation concerns and eroded institutional autonomy</cite><cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Continuous production bureaucracies impede digital innovation</cite><cite id="c6225eae-0">Conglomerate control in Hulu entrenches legacy gatekeeping</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late integrations like Comcast–Netflix and Sky–Netflix preserve bundle economics and legacy interfaces</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundling contrasts with legacy pay-TV, implying modernization reduces lock-in</cite><cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s bundled streaming growth coexists with significant ongoing losses, illustrating trade-offs of platform dependence on legacy cash flows</cite><cite id="c6225eae-2">Disney’s Disney+ case underscores sector concentration and the premium on early brand positioning in SVOD</cite><cite id="c6225eae-4">European domestic SVOD alliances show both promise and structural limits in small markets</cite>.

Title: Television Reshaped by Big Data: Impacts and implications for Netflix-like platforms in the age of dataism
Snippet: The definition of Subscription Video-on-Demand (SVoD) services is similar to OTT television, referring to a service that allows users to access a large range of video content for a monthly rate fee. The quick popularity of such OTT or SVoD services in the US -such as Netflix and Amazonled to a significant number of pay-TV subscribers cancelling their subscriptions, a consumer trend named "cord-cutting": a Nilsen study (2019) estimated that 16 million homes in the US no longer have traditional pay-TV subscriptions, relying exclusively on OTT services or free-to-air terrestrial TV. 

Rather than using the acronyms OTT television or SVoD for services such as Netflix, here the preference is for the term internet-distributed television, defined by Amanda Lotz (2017) as professionally produced content is circulated and consumed through websites, online services, platforms and apps, rather than broadcast, cable, or satellite systems. The major advantage of such services for the audiences are, as observed by Lotz (2017), the personalised viewing of content independent of a schedule, enabling a non-linear consumption of individual content, in contrast with linear TV provided by the traditional TV operators.
</snippet>

Title: The streaming industry and the platform economy: An analysis
Snippet: Streaming platforms can be defined as those whose business model rests on video monetization.They overlap but are distinct from social media platforms that stream videos but whose business case does not entirely rest on them (Cunningham and Craig, 2019).The former includes Facebook Watch, Netflix and YouTube, the latter Facebook, Instagram and Twitter.

Streaming platforms predominantly operate in the field of Video on Demand (VoD), which entails four possible monetization models.Subscription Video on Demand (SVoD) requires members to pay a monthly fee in exchange for unlimited access to the provider's catalogue.With Transactional Video on Demand (TVoD), customers are charged on a per-item basis.Advertising Video on Demand (AVoD) is a model where content is free to access for viewers and content providers sell the audience to advertisers.The AVoD model includes FAST services (Free Ad-supported Streaming Television), which have the particularity of having both linear channels and on-demand content.These services are available on platforms such as Freevee and Pluto TV.Free Video on Demand (FVoD) designates public broadcasters' streaming services.While these organizations are usually financed through licensing fees or tax revenue, FVoD services are freely accessible at the point of watching.

While VoD pre-existed streaming and was developed by cable and satellite pay-TV services (Rooke, 2009: 216-234;Tydeman and Kelm, 1986;Vittet-Philippe, 1999), platforms have brought changes to the monetization formats.Advertising has always been a key revenue stream for broadcasters, but it is streaming that brought AVoD to the forefront of the TV industry in the 2000s.Pay-TV operators have long charged a subscription fee for access, but the concept of charging a (cheaper) fee for an entire catalogue is new to the platform era.Furthermore, SVoD involves less complex contractual arrangements than TV subscription.It is usually unbundled to connection services such as broadband and telephony and can be terminated at short notice.Cable and satellite operators' payper-view is the ancestor of TVoD, which is only used as a payment option within AVoD and SVoD environments.
</snippet>

Title: Authorized and Unauthorized Consumption of SVOD Content: Modeling Determinants of Demand and Measuring Effects of Enforcing Access Control
Snippet: We will first describe the forms of SVOD content consumption and their implications for platforms. As SVOD players differentiate themselves by offering exclusive content and launching new titles directly on their platforms, consumers are probably attracted to a great number of platforms, but subscribing to all of them would imply a high cost. Alternatively, consumers can share the use (and perhaps also the cost) of subscriptions with other households, a practice that violates the terms of service but is relatively common. As an example, 35% of SVOD users in the UK share at least one subscription with others outside of their home [12]. Hence, access to SVOD accounts can basically be done in two ways: through proprietary subscriptions, which are contracted by a household member (subscription holder) and which give the status of authorized users to all household members; and through non-proprietary subscriptions, which are used by members of other households despite being considered as unauthorized users. Another form of unauthorized consumption consists of viewing SVOD content through illegal streaming sites, which provide excellent quality and quick access after the release date on SVOD platforms. Remarkably, unauthorized streaming has become the most popular form of digital piracy: in 2022, illegal streaming sites contributed 95% and 57% of the global piracy of shows and movies, respectively [13]. 

Demand (in number) of proprietary subscriptions, non-proprietary subscriptions, and illegal streaming sites is of great importance for SVOD industry profitability because platforms receive the fees corresponding to the total number of proprietary subscriptions but do not receive any additional revenue from users of non-proprietary subscriptions and illegal streaming sites. In this situation, platforms could start tightening user authentication to hamper account sharing and ultimately encourage new subscriptions. However, such a decision could be a double-edged sword that would deter both authorized and unauthorized use of SVOD accounts [14]. Interestingly, shortly after our fieldwork, Netflix started forcing authentication for users accessing from an unusual location, but the impact of this decision on the number of subscriptions has not been made public.
</snippet>

Title: SVOD Multi-Homing Users in Six Countries: Analyzing Legacy Media Usage, Demographics, Lifestyle, Expectations, and Usage Habits
Snippet: With the surge in streaming service usage, ''multi-homing''-that is, subscription to multiple subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) services simultaneously-is on the rise (Bakos & Halaburda, 2020;Belleflamme & Peitz, 2019;Wu & Chiu, 2023). People in the U.S. subscribe to an average of 4.5 SVODs per month (Gruenwedel, 2022), while in Germany, the average is 3 SVODs per month (Prange, 2021). According to The Guardian, many SVOD subscribers believe that canceling cable television and using only some SVOD services is more economical (Aratani, 2022). However, the monthly cost of subscribing to multiple SVOD services such as Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max can be as high as $50, which is comparable to a basic cable plan's price. On average, U.S. consumers spend $552 annually on streaming services (Orentas & Allen, 2024). Despite the high cost of subscribing to multiple SVOD services, a significant number of global users are subscribed to at least two SVOD services (Gruenwedel, 2022;Orentas & Allen, 2024;Prange, 2021). However, subscriber retention requires SVOD providers to offer reasonable prices. In North America, for instance, Netflix recently increased its prices to increase profits, which resulted in its first decline in subscribers in a decade (Aratani, 2022;Sperling, 2022). Netflix's attempt to stop account sharing has also been received negatively by users (Orentas & Allen, 2024). Netflix's case shows that SVOD providers must attract new subscribers while retaining their existing base by grasping the traits of multi-homing users. 

In today's digital media landscape, consumer behavior generally falls into one of two distinct patterns: ''single-homing,'' that is, preferring a single service, and ''multi-homing,'' that is, subscribing to several services to fulfill diverse needs. Multi-homing users differ from single-homing users in several ways.
</snippet>

Title: Experimental evidence on demand for “on-demand” entertainment
Snippet: The arrival of Netflix and, to a lesser extent, other Subscription Video on Demand (SVoD) services has significantly disrupted traditional media industries with interests in film and television. With SVoD increasing its global penetration, established pay-TV providers have had to reconsider their business and pricing strategies to remain competitive. For example, historic rivals Comcast and Netflix struck a deal in July 2016 to include Netflix in the Comcast X1 set-top box. In March 2018, Europe's Sky pay-TV announced a partnership with Netflix in a bid to retain customers. In November 2014, Australian pay-TV provider Foxtel halved the price of its basic subscription only months before Netflix's arrival.

Anecdotal evidence also suggests that digital piracy (both downloading and streaming) has reduced as a direct result of SVoD alternatives. In 2013, Netflix Chief Content Officer Ted Sarandos made the observation: "When we launch in a territory the Bittorrent traffic drops as the Netflix traffic grows". 1 A number of surveys have also attributed decreased illegal piracy levels to the arrival of Netflix. For example, a 2016 study by the UK Intellectual Property Office related decreased piracy levels to the rising popularity of Netflix. 2 Similar evidence has been found in Australia by the Intellectual Property Awareness Foundation. 3 While few would deny the existence of a SVoD substitution effect against the incumbent providers (both legal and illegal), there have only been limited attempts to measure such effects. In large part, this is likely due to the dearth of data that researchers have access to on consumer activity in this space. Netflix is well known to be extremely protective of its data and, with the exception of the theatrical film industry, sales data from downstream content providers is also extremely difficult to access. Furthermore, obtaining reliable data on illegal piracy presents its own set of challenges, not the least of which being that many participants go to great lengths to conceal their activities.

Presented with these challenges, a revealed-preference analysis of consumer behaviour in these industries is extremely difficult. This study attempts to make headway into this area using laboratory-based stated-preference choice experiments as an alternate approach. Specifically, we investigate how SVoD affects traditional legal and illegal alternatives. Furthermore, our analysis also examines the efficacy of policy designed to curtail digital piracy. We develop a framework in which consumers face choices over viewing alternatives of film

Title: Not Yet the Post-TV Era: Network and MVPD Adaptation to Emergent Distribution Technologies
Snippet: Part of the SVOD classification of online services, Hulu was conceived as a web-based TV distribution portal in 2007; by 2008, the venture was ready for launch to the public and rolled out the red carpet by purchasing an ad during the Super Bowl in early 2009 featuring 30 Rock star Alec Baldwin promoting the service (Stone, 2009). The choice of Baldwin was not a coincidence as Hulu initially grew via partnership with NBCUniversal and News Corp. (owners of Fox) and was given an unspecified amount of money that would be allotted for advertising the nascent platform on networks owned by the media giants (the Super Bowl aired on NBC that year). Hulu also received $100 million in investment capital from Providence Equity Partners in 2007 (James, 2012), a global investment firm which created Newport Television, LLC, a holding company founded for the express purpose of purchasing Clear Channel Communications' 56 television stations. Furthermore, Disney became a partner in 2009, adding content from its family of channels to Hulu (Kramer, 2009); more importantly, though, was the addition of three Disney executives to Hulu's board: Chairman Bob Iger, co-chair Anne Sweeney, and executive vice president Kevin Mayer. Combined with NBCUniversal and News Corp. members, the board of directors at Hulu could be easily mistaken with any traditional television giant's. 

Disney's investment in Hulu was critical to the viability of the platform because it extended the exclusive agreements with NBC and News Corp. whereby only Hulu would have access to content licensed by the investment partners (agreements which were about to expire) for another two years. One final aspect of the Disney deal that exemplified the power wielded by the major media conglomerates was that some of Disney's most popular programming would be initially unavailable on Hulu, including Hannah Montana (2006Montana ( -2011) ) and High School Musical (2006) (Schechner & Holmes, 2009). By denying users its most popular programming, Disney was flexing its muscles and letting it be known in no uncertain terms that traditional television powers would dictate, at the very least, the content available to Hulu users. 

Beyond major media conglomerate investment and executive board occupation, Hulu also follows the adsupported model of American television.
</snippet>

Snippet: Young and highly educated Americans were more likely to be multi-homers than single-homers. Lowincome British were more likely to be light multi-homers, and young and family-oriented British were more likely to be heavy multi-homers than single-homers. 

Young Chinese with high household income and selffulfillment or culture and consumption-focused lifestyles were more likely to be heavy multi-homers than singlehomers. Individuality-oriented Chinese people were more likely to be single-homers. Young Japanese were more likely to be light multi-homers than single-homers, and those young, well-earning with culture and consumptionfocused or individuality-oriented lifestyles were more likely to be heavy multi-homers than single-homers. 

Young Germans were more likely to be light multihomers than single-homers, and those who were young and well-earning with family-oriented lifestyles were more likely to be heavy multi-homers than single-homers. Males and young French were more likely to be light multi-homers than single-homers, and older people with achievement-focused lifestyles were more likely to be single-homers than heavy multi-homers. 

According to this study, multi-homers can be regarded as cord couplers who use both pay TV and SVOD services concurrently depending on their needs and preferences (Jung & Melguizo, 2023), as well as heavy users who enjoy a variety of content via legacy media and SVOD services. Recently, however, many SVOD providers have introduced password-sharing restriction policies to enhance their profitability. Providers such as Netflix, Disney, and Hulu have eliminated password sharing, resulting in increased revenue (Pequen˜o, 2024). However, the increased costs of anti-sharing policies have led to an uptick in the cancellation of subscriptions (Orentas & Allen, 2024). Although Netflix recorded its highest revenue after implementing its anti-sharing policy, the longevity of this success remains uncertain. Similarly, the outlook for other SVOD providers such as Disney, Hulu, and MAX is not very optimistic (Saul, 2024). SVOD operators need to adopt diversified pricing strategies to lock multi-homers into their services.
</snippet>

Title: El mercado del vídeo en streaming: un análisis de la estrategia de Disney+
Snippet: The international launch of Disney+ in November 2019 marked the entry of Disney with its own brand into the market for direct sales of subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) consumer services. This market, although with Netflix as a prominent leader, is still in a consolidation phase that could lead to the disappearance of many operators since although traditional pay TV operators, such as cable operators in the US, are developing their own platforms due to subscriber loss in their core business, all face new threats such as increased operating costs, the need to increase investment in own production and others derived from new consumption habits such as consumer fatigue. This article analyzes, through the applied case study methodology, Disney’s strategy to position Disney+ successfully in a short period of time and confirms findings from previous studies on the nature and evolution of the sector and trends like its high degree of concentration. which points to the complex reality of the SVOD market, the value that global brands would continue to have at this stage and finally allows us to analyze the real possibilities of creating a new streaming video market with lower entry barriers.


Resumen
El lanzamiento internacional de Disney+ en noviembre del 2019 significó la entrada de Disney con una marca propia en el mercado de la venta directa de servicios al consumidor de vídeo bajo demanda por suscripción (SVOD). Este mercado, aunque con Netflix como líder destacado, se encuentra en una fase de consolidación que podría llevar a la desaparición de muchos operadores, ya que aunque las cadenas de TV de pago, como los cableoperadores en EUA, están creando sus propias plataformas por la pérdida de abonados en su negocio principal, todos se enfrentan a nuevas amenazas como el aumento de los costes de operación, la necesidad de incrementar la inversión en producción propia y otras derivadas de los nuevos hábitos de consumo como la fatiga del consumidor. Este articulo analiza, mediante la metodología del caso
</snippet>

Title: Balancing Tradition and Digital: Challenges, Opportunities in Disney's Business Model Reconstruction and Implications for Legacy Media Conglomerates
Snippet: Streaming media has emerged as a critical growth vector for The Walt Disney Company, representing a strategic shift in response to secular declines in traditional cable and theatrical distribution. The migration of audiences from linear television to digital platforms is exemplified by ESPN's subscriber erosion, falling from 100 million in 2011 to approximately 74 million by 2023 [4]. In reaction to these industry dynamics, Disney deployed an aggressive streaming strategy centered on the launch of Disney+ and its subsequent bundling with Hulu and ESPN+. This approach facilitated an unprecedented acceleration in subscriber acquisition, with Disney+ attaining 100 million subscribers within 16 months-a milestone that required a decade for Netflix to achieve [5]. 

Nevertheless, this rapid expansion entailed significant strategic trade-offs. The company's Premier Access initiative, which generated an estimated $900 million in revenue during 2021 [6], provoked considerable channel conflict with established theatrical exhibition partners. Empirical evidence indicates that hybrid release strategies correlated with a 57% decline in per-screen revenue for Disney films during the latter half of 2021 [7]. The subsequent discontinuation of Premier Access in 2022 underscores the inherent tensions between digital distribution innovation and the preservation of legacy exhibition relationships. 

From a financial perspective, Disney's direct-to-consumer segment has demonstrated substantial revenue growth, reaching $20.5 billion in fiscal year 2023 [2]. However, the segment continues to face profitability challenges, with streaming operations reporting aggregate losses of $4.2 billion during the same period. This dichotomy highlights a fundamental strategic dilemma: while streaming services constitute an essential component of Disney's future growth trajectory, their development remains financially dependent on cash flows generated by traditional business segments, particularly theme parks and linear networks.
</snippet>

Title: ‘If you can’t beat them, be them’
Snippet: Faced with heavy competition of global subscription-video-on-demand (SVOD) streaming services, along with increased pressure on fi nancing and distribution of domestic content, legacy media players are increasingly exploring the potential of local SVOD services as domestic alternatives to global platforms such as Netflix and Disney+, often in collaboration with other European broadcasters and/or distributors.This article presents an in-depth case study of Streamz, a domestic SVOD alternative launched in Belgium in September 2020. Building on scholarly work on media disruption and platform power, the case study examines the political and market context that shaped the existence of the platform, and critically analyses the strategies pursued by legacy media players in attempting to develop and emulate key competitive advantages of global SVOD players. The article demonstrates how a persistent policy push to collaborate in a small market resulted in an unusual joint venture and, at the same time, how diff erent market factors, most of them characteristic for small media markets, pose signifi cant challenges for domestic players to develop a profi table platform in Europe, let alone be able to stand achance in a highly competitive streaming market.

Summary
Traditional broadcasters’ early responses to SVOD (2010–2015)—mixing mimicry (multiscreen apps and “catch‑up”), strategic collaboration (platform joint ventures and paid partnerships), and resistance (bundle defense and pricing hold‑ups)—created organizational and technological lock‑in that now limits competitive options. Evidence spans organizational path dependencies (bureaucracy and linear production routines), governance overreach that entrenches legacy control, late and bundle‑tied integrations with SVODs, and market‑level network effects that make exit costly. Alternative early choices—earlier standalone SVOD launches, neutral platform governance, studio‑direct distribution, ad‑supported experimentation, and modernized conditional access/API ecosystems—would have reduced lock‑in and positioned incumbents better, though they carry their own trade‑offs.

Organizational lock‑in: routines, governance, and delayed capability building
- Broadcasters and public service broadcasters gravitated toward “mimicry” and “strategic collaboration” with SVODs rather than systematic reinvention of production and distribution logic, adopting streaming production culture and partnerships to appear adaptive while facing concerns over “platformisation” that erode institutional roles and funding stability <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Traditional broadcasters adopted strategic responses to SVODs including mimicry and strategic collaboration, raising concerns about platformisation and the erosion of public service roles and funding</cite>. 
- Organizational architectures built for continuous linear production and centralized hierarchies (e.g., in‑house broadcasters) are structurally conservative: continuous production lines and bureaucracies blunt innovation incentives, making flexible specialization for digital demand harder to embed without long‑run capability lock‑in <cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Introducing innovation is difficult in organizations where continuous production is paramount, with bureaucracies focused on a continuous stream of programmes, impeding change toward demand-driven digital models</cite>. 
- Governance overreach can entrench lock‑in: Disney’s early investment in Hulu simultaneously deepened control via board dominance and exclusive licensing that shielded legacy networks, signaling that SVOD access would be mediated by traditional TV power, with popular Disney hits initially withheld from Hulu to assert leverage <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s board appointments and exclusive licensing extended legacy control over Hulu, with popular Disney programming initially unavailable on Hulu to signal traditional TV powers would dictate content available to SVOD users</cite>. 
- Market‑level network effects and pricing power reinforce incumbents’ platforms: SVODs altered monetization formats and unbundled subscriptions, but pay‑TV operators’ historical bundles and relationships created path dependencies; when pressure mounted, late deals (e.g., Comcast–Netflix in 2016; Sky–Netflix in 2018; Foxtel price cuts in 2014) were driven by bundle defense and pricing competition, underscoring late, reactive integration with legacy set‑top boxes and pay‑TV pricing rather than first‑party OTT refactoring <cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundled subscriptions and simplified contracts relative to pay-TV, bringing AVoD to the forefront and making SVOD less tightly coupled to cable/satellite infrastructure than legacy pay-per-view</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-4">Comcast and Netflix struck a deal in July 2016 to include Netflix in the Comcast X1 set-top box; Sky partnered with Netflix in 2018 to retain customers; Foxtel halved basic subscription pricing months before Netflix’s arrival</cite>. 
- Consumer multi‑homing and platform pricing policies create sticky ecosystems: as SVODs expand, users subscribe to multiple platforms and legacy media “cord‑couple” to hybrid bundles; anti‑sharing enforcement increases revenue but risks cancellations, illustrating how pricing and access control bind users and firms into overlapping networks—raising exit and platform‑switching costs <cite id="1e32db7b-3">Multi-homing is rising, with many subscribing to multiple SVODs; SVOD operators are adopting password-sharing restrictions to lock in users, though increased costs can spur cancellations</cite><cite id="c6225eae-1">Providers such as Netflix, Disney, and Hulu eliminated password sharing to enhance profitability, but the policy trade-offs raise subscription cancellation risks and uncertainty about long-run viability</cite>.

Technological lock‑in: delivery pipelines, DRM, and late platform integration
- Pay‑TV operators’ reliance on proprietary set‑top environments and bundled pricing delayed true OTT refactoring: forced integrations like Netflix in X1 and Sky’s late partnerships embedded SVOD into legacy interfaces, preserving linear bundling economics and data silos, which restricts agile, consumer‑first experimentation and data‑driven personalization that scale with pure SVODs <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late partnerships (Comcast–Netflix, Sky–Netflix) and Foxtel price cuts were responses to cord-cutting pressures, embedding SVOD into legacy set-top boxes and pay-TV pricing structures</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD typically unbundles to broadband/telephony and can be terminated at short notice, contrasting with pay-TV’s bundled infrastructure and complex legacy contracts</cite>. 
- Governance‑by‑conglomerate ownership and board control in early Hulu deepened platform coupling to legacy scheduling and advertising logics; content exclusivity and gatekeeping signaled that SVOD access remains a lever of traditional power, discouraging neutral, open platform approaches that could have reduced lock‑in <cite id="c6225eae-0">Hulu’s board included top Disney/NBC/News Corp executives, and Disney withheld popular programming to demonstrate traditional television powers would dictate Hulu’s content</cite>. 
- Market structure and data/monetization shifts are locked in by two‑sided platform designs: AVoD’s rise foregrounded advertising as a core revenue stream; SVOD’s subscription unbundling and flexible packaging altered legacy relationships with advertisers and distributors, but incumbents’ late moves to integrate SVODs into existing ad systems and distribution channels constrained experimentation with pure ad‑supported and data‑native models <cite id="1e32db7b-1">Advertising became a key revenue stream in the streaming era; SVOD’s subscription unbundling and simpler contracts contrasted with legacy pay-TV and PPV models</cite>. 
- Platformization and content control raise institutional risks: as broadcasters “build like platforms” via partnerships and in‑house apps, they risk ceding distribution power to platforms while retaining content control, creating dependency on platform gateways and pricing policies that limit autonomy and responsiveness <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Mimicking SVOD strategies and engaging in strategic collaborations raised concerns about platformisation of culture and the erosion of public service broadcasters’ roles</cite>.

Evidence that alternative early choices would have positioned incumbents better
- Earlier, more aggressive standalone SVOD entry by studios and networks: Disney’s later success with Disney+ and its bundled acceleration (100 million subscribers in 16 months) relied on a direct consumer stack that only emerged after sustained linear losses; had Disney earlier prioritized studio‑direct SVOD alongside linear networks, it would have de‑coupled distribution faster and reduced reliance on cash flows from theme parks and linear ads, though with similar content‑control trade‑offs <cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s direct-to-consumer streaming segment grew to $20.5B in FY2023 but reported aggregate streaming losses of $4.2B, highlighting financial dependence on traditional segments even as streaming accelerates</cite><cite id="c6225eae-2">Disney’s 2019 Disney+ launch into a consolidating SVOD market illustrates high sector concentration and the premium on global brands, supporting earlier direct SVOD positioning as a strategic lever</cite>. 
- Neutral platform governance and open ecosystems: European legacy players’ joint domestic platform (Streamz) shows that early collaboration to emulate core advantages of global platforms is possible but constrained by small‑market politics and capital, underscoring how governance design and funding structures can either reduce or deepen lock‑in; neutral, open APIs and de‑verticalized access would have mitigated proprietary lock‑in with Netflix/Disney and preserved competition <cite id="c6225eae-4">Legacy media collaboration on a domestic SVOD (Streamz) illustrates how policy-driven collaboration can create a joint venture but faces significant challenges in a highly competitive market, limiting the platform’s ability to stand a chance</cite>. 
- Pay‑TV modernization and MVPD adaptation: early investment in conditional‑access refactoring, neutral MVPD APIs, and data/identity layers would have enabled smoother OTT aggregation and multi‑home support rather than forcing late integrations like Netflix in X1/Sky, which preserved linear bundles and slowed personalized, cross‑screen experiences <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Comcast’s inclusion of Netflix in X1 and Sky’s partnership with Netflix reflect late-stage integrations driven by bundle protection and pricing competition</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD’s unbundling and termination flexibility contrast with legacy pay-TV’s bundled infrastructure, suggesting earlier modernization would reduce coupling</cite>. 
- Studio‑direct consumer stacks and ad‑supported experimentation: Disney’s Premier Access hybrid model highlighted tensions between digital innovation and legacy theatrical partners; earlier, studio‑centric direct-to-consumer launch and ad‑supported SVOD experimentation would have reduced dependence on theatrical gatekeepers and diversified monetization, though with profitability risks and distribution conflicts <cite id="c6225eae-3">Hybrid release strategies correlated with a 57% decline in per-screen revenue for Disney films in H2 2021, and Premier Access was discontinued in 2022, revealing tensions between digital innovation and legacy exhibition</cite>. 
- Consumer‑first pricing and access models: early adoption of flexible, multi‑home pricing and password‑sharing policies that balance retention and revenue (instead of heavy anti‑sharing) can lock users into bundles without mass churn, while late anti‑sharing shocks raise cancellation risk; learning from Netflix’s mixed outcomes, incumbents could have blended ad‑supported tiers and subsidized bundles to reduce lock‑in costs for consumers <cite id="1e32db7b-3">SVOD providers’ elimination of password sharing increased revenue but raised cancellation risks, showing policy trade-offs in locking in multi-homing users</cite><cite id="c6225eae-1">Anti-sharing policies can strengthen user lock-in but may undermine longevity, suggesting diversified pricing strategies to retain multi-homers</cite>. 
- Content strategy choices: early exclusives to attract subscribers (as Netflix built originals) versus late exclusives can create different platform power; Disney’s strategic withholding and gatekeeping in Hulu signaled traditional control and slowed balanced market competition, whereas earlier, reciprocal access and cross‑platform originals would have de‑risked user acquisition and reduced lock‑in <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s early Hulu deal withheld popular programming and emphasized board control, signaling that SVOD content access would be dictated by traditional TV powers</cite>. 
- Regional collaborations and distribution parity: early European alliances (e.g., Sky/Canal+/Netflix deals) show incumbents could have used joint ventures to grant parity of access across legacy networks, preventing single‑source dependence and creating competitive internal platforms; however, small‑market cases like Belgium’s Streamz demonstrate funding and policy constraints that still limit alternatives <cite id="c6225eae-4">Belgian legacy players’ joint venture (Streamz) shows policy-driven collaboration can create domestic platforms but faces significant market challenges in standing against global competitors</cite>. 

Mechanisms that limit options and suggest lock‑in
- Governance and control: Conglomerate ownership and board capture in early SVODs locked decision rights in legacy divisions, aligning platform strategy to preserve linear ad sales and bundling rather than consumer‑centered OTT, creating durable path dependence <cite id="c6225eae-0">Hulu’s board included top executives from NBCUniversal, News Corp, and Disney, with Disney withholding popular programming to assert control</cite>. 
- Network effects and two‑sided markets: SVOD’s unbundling and AVoD/FAST hybrids reframed audience and ad monetization; incumbents’ late integration deepened two‑sided dependencies with distributors and advertisers, while platform network effects bind users across overlapping SVODs and legacy bundles, raising switching costs <cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundling and AVoD’s rise reframed monetization; SVOD’s simpler unbundling contrasts with pay-TV’s complex legacy contracts</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-3">Rising multi-homing and platform pricing policies illustrate how lock-in operates across overlapping SVOD ecosystems</cite>. 
- Consumer behavior and pricing: The rise of multi‑homing and the sensitivity of SVOD churn to pricing and access policies mean incumbents must diversify and align pricing across linear and digital, or risk binding users into costly anti‑sharing regimes that backfire <cite id="1e32db7b-3">U.S. and German consumers subscribe to multiple SVODs on the rise; anti-sharing policies can raise revenue but trigger cancellations</cite>. 
- Organizational inertia: Continuous linear production and bureaucratic structures impede rapid reorientation toward demand‑driven, multiscreen production and data‑native operations, entrenching technological and organizational lock‑in <cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Organizations built for continuous linear production develop bureaucracies that impede innovation and flexible specialization for digital demand</cite>. 

What would have been better early choices and their trade‑offs
- Build neutral, open consumer platforms: Early MVPD‑neutral APIs, conditional‑access decoupling, and open identity/data layers would have allowed aggregation across legacy and SVOD catalogs without embedding content in proprietary set‑top gateways, improving user experience and retention while preserving competition; however, short‑term revenue synergies with SVOD licensors and bundle defenses made such openness politically and financially difficult <cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late integrations like Netflix in X1 and Sky’s deals reflected bundle defense; earlier neutral APIs would have reduced gateway lock-in</cite>. 
- Studio‑centric direct distribution: Earlier Disney/Time‑Warner/CBS studio‑direct SVOD (e.g., branded tiers) would have accelerated acquisition and diversified revenue beyond linear ads; Disney’s experience shows rapid growth but persistent losses and conflicts with legacy exhibition, underscoring the need to balance near‑term profitability with long‑run platform investment and content‑studio relations <cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s streaming segment grew to $20.5B but reported $4.2B aggregate losses in FY2023, revealing the trade-off between growth and profitability in a DCI-dependent model</cite>. 
- Ad‑supported experimentation and diversified pricing: Early ad‑supported SVOD tiers and family‑shared plans to capture multi‑homing behavior would have reduced per‑user costs and dependence on paid password sharing; evidence shows anti‑sharing can raise revenue but also increase churn, so earlier diversified pricing would have balanced retention and monetization <cite id="1e32db7b-3">Multi-homing users increasingly subscribe to multiple SVODs; diversified pricing is needed to lock in users while mitigating the negative effects of anti-sharing policies</cite>. 
- Governance that de‑verticalizes platform control: Avoiding board capture and exclusive licensing that prioritize legacy gateways would have enabled more balanced access and faster data/monetization innovation; Disney’s early Hulu governance illustrates the opposite—content gatekeeping and board dominance that slowed parity and reinforced linear control <cite id="c6225eae-0">Disney’s governance and exclusivity in Hulu signaled that SVOD access would be dictated by traditional TV powers</cite>. 
- Regional alliances with parity: Early European alliances (e.g., Sky/Canal+/Netflix) that grant equal access across legacy platforms and domestic SVODs could prevent single‑source dependence and foster competitive internal platforms; the Belgian Streamz case shows that while such choices are possible, funding, market size, and policy constraints limit scalability <cite id="c6225eae-4">Legacy players’ collaboration on Streamz shows policy and market constraints make profitable parity platforms hard to scale in small markets</cite>. 

Conclusion
The initial strategic responses of traditional broadcasters—mimicry, collaboration, and bundle‑defense—locked them into hybrid organizational and technological architectures that privilege legacy gateways and governance over consumer‑first platform design. Evidence from Disney/Hulu governance, late pay‑TV integrations with Netflix, organizational production bureaucracies, and market‑level network effects shows durable lock‑in in delivery pipelines, pricing, and content control. Alternative early choices—neutral MVPD platforms and APIs, studio‑direct SVOD launches with diversified pricing, ad‑supported experimentation, and de‑verticalized governance—would have reduced lock‑in, improved competitive positioning, and aligned incentives to monetize multi‑homing users; however, incumbents faced strong internal and external path dependencies that favored short‑term bundle preservation over long‑term platform freedom, producing the hybrid models we see today with both growth and persistent profitability headwinds <cite id="91bb8fc4-0">Mimicry and collaboration with SVODs raised platformisation concerns and eroded institutional autonomy</cite><cite id="91bb8fc4-4">Continuous production bureaucracies impede digital innovation</cite><cite id="c6225eae-0">Conglomerate control in Hulu entrenches legacy gatekeeping</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-4">Late integrations like Comcast–Netflix and Sky–Netflix preserve bundle economics and legacy interfaces</cite><cite id="1e32db7b-1">SVOD unbundling contrasts with legacy pay-TV, implying modernization reduces lock-in</cite><cite id="c6225eae-3">Disney’s bundled streaming growth coexists with significant ongoing losses, illustrating trade-offs of platform dependence on legacy cash flows</cite><cite id="c6225eae-2">Disney’s Disney+ case underscores sector concentration and the premium on early brand positioning in SVOD</cite><cite id="c6225eae-4">European domestic SVOD alliances show both promise and structural limits in small markets</cite>.</answer>

Title: ‘Being a drama producer is not in the least artistic work’ – Adopting streaming production culture at the Finnish public service broadcaster
Snippet: The changes observed in Yle's drama production can be interpreted by applying the five strategic responses identified by D' Arma et al. (2021), which describe how public service media organisations have reacted to the rise of SVODs. These responses include: complacency (ignoring the threats posed by streaming services), resistance (attempting to preserve the status quo), differentiation (adjusting content to stand out from competitors), mimicry (expanding operations to new platforms), and strategic collaboration (partnering with SVOD services). As this article has shown, Yle has primarily responded to the global transformations in television by mimicking SVOD strategies and engaging in strategic collaborations with streaming platforms. 

This trajectory raises concerns about the platformisation of culture. While the adoption of a streaming production culture at Yle can be justified as an adaptive strategy to ensure the existence of Finland's public service broadcaster, it also challenges the traditional role of public service broadcasters as national cultural institutions. As Yle's funding and role in the digital media environment continue to be debated, there is a pressing need for a broader public discussion on the future of public service broadcasting and its place in Finnish cultural life.

Title: Users’ Satisfaction Regarding Continuance Intention of Subscription Video-on-Demand Platforms for Watching Football Matches: A Stimulus-Organism-Response Perspective
Snippet: This study aims to fill the research gap from previous studies by analyzing factors that may influence users' satisfaction regarding the intention to continue using SVoD to watch football broadcasts. In this study, we adopted two theoretical models commonly used in previous research-the expectation confirmation model (ECM) and the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) model-to analyze the intention to continue using the SVoD platform. ECM has been used in various research contexts to measure satisfaction levels and to determine the factors that influence users to repurchase a product or service (Pereira & Tam, 2021). In this study, the S-O-R model was used because it fits the environment under study, in which an object is given to someone in the form of an SVoD application and that person has a response or impression of what they can do with that object. We used S-O-R to analyze how the interaction between stimulus, organism, and response can affect individual behavior and responses in the studied environment. This research is also expected to help SVoD service users find a quality and legal SVoD platform to watch football broadcasts, thus increasing their intention to continue using SVoD services to access football broadcasts.

Title: Slow Television
Snippet: Television is changing -digitization, new platforms and increased competition are undermining traditional ways of producing television. In the post-television era new ways of reaching and engaging viewers are being sought in order to stand out in the ever-intensifying battle to win viewers' attention. One of the strategies that commercial channels have used in particular is the introduction of different reality concepts in which ordinary people participate in situations that are often unreal. Some of these concepts, such as Big Brother or Pop Idol, gradually escalate and culminate in an event-like finale. Unlike classic media events (Dayan & Katz 1992), these are organized by television. Kjus (2008) coined the term 'event-media' for these concepts, where different platforms -television, the Internet, mobile phones -collaborate and viewers are involved in participatory activities (e.g., voting). 

Much of the ongoing academic discussion on public-service broadcasting has to do with convergence and the change from public-service broadcasting to public-service media (cf. Lowe & Hujanen 2003, Lowe & Bardoel 2007, Lowe 2010). Content innovation has been largely overlooked. Public-service broadcasters must also seek innovative ways to fulfil their public-service functions in an increasingly competitive environment (Wurff & Leenders 2008). They too may engage in event media, but they are more re-10.1515/nor-2015-0008 stricted than commercial actors are, because they are supposed to pursue democratic, ethical and national values rather than market success. 

In-house production companies like the BBC or the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation (NRK) are in a special situation. Introducing innovation may be difficult in an organization in which continuous production is paramount (Christensen 2008). Creative production, such as film, is often organized by means of flexible specialization (Lorenzen 2009). Whereas commercial channels obtain flexibility by outsourcing production, inhouse production companies tend to develop bureaucracies that are more focused on the production of a continuous stream of programmes.

Title: Television Reshaped by Big Data: Impacts and implications for Netflix-like platforms in the age of dataism
Snippet: The definition of Subscription Video-on-Demand (SVoD) services is similar to OTT television, referring to a service that allows users to access a large range of video content for a monthly rate fee. The quick popularity of such OTT or SVoD services in the US -such as Netflix and Amazonled to a significant number of pay-TV subscribers cancelling their subscriptions, a consumer trend named "cord-cutting": a Nilsen study (2019) estimated that 16 million homes in the US no longer have traditional pay-TV subscriptions, relying exclusively on OTT services or free-to-air terrestrial TV. 

Rather than using the acronyms OTT television or SVoD for services such as Netflix, here the preference is for the term internet-distributed television, defined by Amanda Lotz (2017) as professionally produced content is circulated and consumed through websites, online services, platforms and apps, rather than broadcast, cable, or satellite systems. The major advantage of such services for the audiences are, as observed by Lotz (2017), the personalised viewing of content independent of a schedule, enabling a non-linear consumption of individual content, in contrast with linear TV provided by the traditional TV operators.

Title: The streaming industry and the platform economy: An analysis
Snippet: Streaming platforms can be defined as those whose business model rests on video monetization.They overlap but are distinct from social media platforms that stream videos but whose business case does not entirely rest on them (Cunningham and Craig, 2019).The former includes Facebook Watch, Netflix and YouTube, the latter Facebook, Instagram and Twitter.

Streaming platforms predominantly operate in the field of Video on Demand (VoD), which entails four possible monetization models.Subscription Video on Demand (SVoD) requires members to pay a monthly fee in exchange for unlimited access to the provider's catalogue.With Transactional Video on Demand (TVoD), customers are charged on a per-item basis.Advertising Video on Demand (AVoD) is a model where content is free to access for viewers and content providers sell the audience to advertisers.The AVoD model includes FAST services (Free Ad-supported Streaming Television), which have the particularity of having both linear channels and on-demand content.These services are available on platforms such as Freevee and Pluto TV.Free Video on Demand (FVoD) designates public broadcasters' streaming services.While these organizations are usually financed through licensing fees or tax revenue, FVoD services are freely accessible at the point of watching.

While VoD pre-existed streaming and was developed by cable and satellite pay-TV services (Rooke, 2009: 216-234;Tydeman and Kelm, 1986;Vittet-Philippe, 1999), platforms have brought changes to the monetization formats.Advertising has always been a key revenue stream for broadcasters, but it is streaming that brought AVoD to the forefront of the TV industry in the 2000s.Pay-TV operators have long charged a subscription fee for access, but the concept of charging a (cheaper) fee for an entire catalogue is new to the platform era.Furthermore, SVoD involves less complex contractual arrangements than TV subscription.It is usually unbundled to connection services such as broadband and telephony and can be terminated at short notice.Cable and satellite operators' payper-view is the ancestor of TVoD, which is only used as a payment option within AVoD and SVoD environments.

Title: Authorized and Unauthorized Consumption of SVOD Content: Modeling Determinants of Demand and Measuring Effects of Enforcing Access Control
Snippet: We will first describe the forms of SVOD content consumption and their implications for platforms. As SVOD players differentiate themselves by offering exclusive content and launching new titles directly on their platforms, consumers are probably attracted to a great number of platforms, but subscribing to all of them would imply a high cost. Alternatively, consumers can share the use (and perhaps also the cost) of subscriptions with other households, a practice that violates the terms of service but is relatively common. As an example, 35% of SVOD users in the UK share at least one subscription with others outside of their home [12]. Hence, access to SVOD accounts can basically be done in two ways: through proprietary subscriptions, which are contracted by a household member (subscription holder) and which give the status of authorized users to all household members; and through non-proprietary subscriptions, which are used by members of other households despite being considered as unauthorized users. Another form of unauthorized consumption consists of viewing SVOD content through illegal streaming sites, which provide excellent quality and quick access after the release date on SVOD platforms. Remarkably, unauthorized streaming has become the most popular form of digital piracy: in 2022, illegal streaming sites contributed 95% and 57% of the global piracy of shows and movies, respectively [13]. 

Demand (in number) of proprietary subscriptions, non-proprietary subscriptions, and illegal streaming sites is of great importance for SVOD industry profitability because platforms receive the fees corresponding to the total number of proprietary subscriptions but do not receive any additional revenue from users of non-proprietary subscriptions and illegal streaming sites. In this situation, platforms could start tightening user authentication to hamper account sharing and ultimately encourage new subscriptions. The definition of Subscription Video-on-Demand (SVoD) services is similar to OTT television, referring to a service that allows users to access a large range of video content for a monthly rate fee. The quick popularity of such OTT or SVoD services in the US -such as Netflix and Amazonled to a significant number of pay-TV subscribers cancelling their subscriptions, a consumer trend named "cord-cutting": a Nilsen study (2019) estimated that 16 million homes in the US no longer have traditional pay-TV subscriptions, relying exclusively on OTT services or free-to-air terrestrial TV. 

Rather than using the acronyms OTT television or SVoD for services such as Netflix, here the preference is for the term internet-distributed television, defined by Amanda Lotz (2017) as professionally produced content is circulated and consumed through websites, online services, platforms and apps, rather than broadcast, cable, or satellite systems. The major advantage of such services for the audiences are, as observed by Lotz (2017), the personalised viewing of content independent of a schedule, enabling a non-linear consumption of individual content, in contrast with linear TV provided by the traditional TV operators.

Streaming platforms can be defined as those whose business model rests on video monetization.They overlap but are distinct from social media platforms that stream videos but whose business case does not entirely rest on them (Cunningham and Craig, 2019).The former includes Facebook Watch, Netflix and YouTube, the latter Facebook, Instagram and Twitter.

Streaming platforms predominantly operate in the field of Video on Demand (VoD), which entails four possible monetization models.Subscription Video on Demand (SVoD) requires members to pay a monthly fee in exchange for unlimited access to the provider's catalogue.With Transactional Video on Demand (TVoD), customers are charged on a per-item basis.Advertising Video on Demand (AVoD) is a model where content is free to access for viewers and content providers sell the audience to advertisers.The AVoD model includes FAST services (Free Ad-supported Streaming Television), which have the particularity of having both linear channels and on-demand content.These services are available on platforms such as Freevee and Pluto TV.Free Video on Demand (FVoD) designates public broadcasters' streaming services.While these organizations are usually financed through licensing fees or tax revenue, FVoD services are freely accessible at the point of watching.

While VoD pre-existed streaming and was developed by cable and satellite pay-TV services (Rooke, 2009: 216-234;Tydeman and Kelm, 1986;Vittet-Philippe, 1999), platforms have brought changes to the monetization formats.Advertising has always been a key revenue stream for broadcasters, but it is streaming that brought AVoD to the forefront of the TV industry in the 2000s.Pay-TV operators have long charged a subscription fee for access, but the concept of charging a (cheaper) fee for an entire catalogue is new to the platform era.Furthermore, SVoD involves less complex contractual arrangements than TV subscription.It is usually unbundled to connection services such as broadband and telephony and can be terminated at short notice.Cable and satellite operators' payper-view is the ancestor of TVoD, which is only used as a payment option within AVoD and SVoD environments.

We will first describe the forms of SVOD content consumption and their implications for platforms. As SVOD players differentiate themselves by offering exclusive content and launching new titles directly on their platforms, consumers are probably attracted to a great number of platforms, but subscribing to all of them would imply a high cost. Alternatively, consumers can share the use (and perhaps also the cost) of subscriptions with other households, a practice that violates the terms of service but is relatively common. As an example, 35% of SVOD users in the UK share at least one subscription with others outside of their home [12]. Another form of unauthorized consumption consists of viewing SVOD content through illegal streaming sites, which provide excellent quality and quick access after the release date on SVOD platforms. Remarkably, unauthorized streaming has become the most popular form of digital piracy: in 2022, illegal streaming sites contributed 95% and 57% of the global piracy of shows and movies, respectively [13].
